CHAPTER 011 / 10

CHAPTER 01

What one training example means

An ads or recommendation model learns from past interactions so that it can score a future opportunity: given this user, this candidate item, and this situation, how likely is a particular outcome? This guide starts with click prediction, then explains retrieval, ratings, conversions, and sequence prediction. You need no prior knowledge of recommendation systems. A neural network is a model with adjustable numbers called parameters; training changes those numbers to reduce an error score called the loss. Technical terms are explained as they appear and collected in the glossary.

An item is the thing being recommended: an ad, product, video, article, or song. A candidate is an item being considered. An impression is a logged showing of an item under your system's exposure definition. A click is one possible response to that impression. Serving means running a trained model on live requests.

For a click prediction model, one training example usually describes one item shown to one user at one time, plus whether that showing led to at least one valid click within a defined window. CTR, or click-through rate, is clicked impressions divided by impressions under that binary-label rule. pCTR is the model's predicted probability of a click.

User Candidate shown Situation at display time Outcome
U7 Running shoe ad A42 Mobile home feed at 10 AM UTC Clicked
U7 Camera ad A81 Mobile home feed at 10 AM UTC Did not click
U9 Running shoe ad A42 Desktop at 8 PM UTC Did not click

These rows are invented teaching examples. The same user and the same ad can occur many times; each showing is a distinct event.

The information used to make a prediction is called the features, often written as x. The answer used to teach the model is the label, often written as y. For click prediction, y=1 means clicked and y=0 means not clicked under the chosen rule.

x = user information + candidate information + context + earlier behavior
y = observed outcome after this opportunity

model(x) = estimated probability of a click

An output of 0.03 is intended as a 3% click probability. A calibrated model is one whose probabilities agree with observed frequencies: across many comparable opportunities scored near 0.03, roughly 3% should receive a click. Calibration must be checked on the population where the model is used; sampled training data can distort it. An individual prediction is not a guarantee.

There are three distinct representations to keep straight:

Representation What it contains
Raw logs Events such as impressions, clicks, purchases, and page views
Training records Joined features, labels, and bookkeeping for each example
Model tensors Numerical arrays with specified shapes and types that the model computes on

A CSV file, a JSON record, and a Parquet table can all represent the same logical examples. The file extension does not determine what the model learns, provided the loader preserves types and values. For example, a CSV reader must not discard leading zeros in IDs or silently conflate missing values with empty strings. CSV is a text table format; JSON represents named fields and lists; Parquet stores typed table columns efficiently.

Raw events→Training records→Encoded batches→Model + labels

CHAPTER 02

From raw events to training rows

The information usually lives in several tables

A web application does not normally log a complete neural-network input whenever someone clicks. It records different events and maintains separate information about users and items. A training pipeline combines them.

The following tables are an invented miniature shopping app.

Impressions

impression_id  request_id  user_id  item_id  shown_at              surface
imp_101        req_10      U7       A42      2026-11-01T10:00:00Z  home_feed
imp_102        req_10      U7       A81      2026-11-01T10:00:00Z  home_feed

Requests

request_id  scored_at             device  surface
req_10      2026-11-01T09:59:58Z  mobile  home_feed

Clicks

impression_id  clicked_at
imp_101        2026-11-01T10:00:05Z

Item information available at the time

item_id  category  price   valid_from            valid_to
A42      shoes     80.00   2026-10-20T00:00:00Z  2026-11-01T12:00:00Z
A42      shoes     65.00   2026-11-01T12:00:00Z  (open)
A81      cameras   300.00  2026-10-20T00:00:00Z  (open)

Earlier user behavior

user_id  item_id  category  action  occurred_at           available_at
U7       A12      shoes     view    2026-11-01T09:40:00Z  2026-11-01T09:40:02Z
U7       A18      shoes     view    2026-11-01T09:50:00Z  2026-11-01T09:50:02Z
U7       A33      books     view    2026-11-01T09:55:00Z  2026-11-01T09:55:02Z

How one row is assembled

A request asks the system to choose recommendations. The model scores req_10 at 09:59:58; the two impressions are logged as shown at 10:00:00. For imp_101, attach the information about U7 and A42, the device and surface from the request, and behavior available before 09:59:58. The training record stores the request's scored_at as prediction_time. All timestamps here use UTC, a common worldwide time reference; the Z suffix marks UTC. After the click observation window closes, attach the label.

For this example, assume a 30-minute click window starting at shown_at, with the start included and end excluded. Allow another five minutes for click logs to arrive; both labels are final at 10:35. A positive example has label 1; a negative example has label 0. The valid click at 10:00:05 makes imp_101 positive. With no valid attributed click in its window, imp_102 is negative after finalization. These durations are teaching assumptions, not universal rules. Multiple valid clicks on one impression still produce one binary label.

Attribution is the rule assigning an outcome to an impression or click. Here a shared impression identifier makes it simple; the chapter on recommendation tasks explains how ad platforms attribute conversions that happen later on another website or app. Deduplication removes repeated copies of the same event; it must not erase distinct showings.

Join response events using an impression identifier or an explicitly defined attribution rule. Joining on user ID and item ID alone can attach one click to several different showings.

The time boundary is part of the format

For the 10:00 impression scored at 09:59:58:

  • Features must represent information the scoring system could have used at its decision time.

  • Historical behavior must stop before that decision.

  • The response label can use later events inside its specified window.

  • A count such as “clicks in the last seven days” must be computed as of that decision, not as of the day you build the dataset.

Including the 10:00:05 click in the history used to predict that same click is data leakage: the answer has slipped into the question.

Time matters for item and user metadata too. If an item's price changed at noon, the 10:00 training row should not silently use the noon price. Delayed event arrival also matters: a behavior that occurred at 09:59:00 but reached your system at 10:02 was unavailable when the 10:00 impression was scored at 09:59:58.

Matching records across tables is a join. A point-in-time join selects information valid and available at the scoring cutoff. In this example, require both occurred_at < scored_at and available_at < scored_at for history. Pick the item version whose interval includes scored_at: valid_from is inclusive and valid_to exclusive. The metadata table assumes each version was available from valid_from; if corrections arrive later, also record when each version became available.

Fields used for joining and auditing do not automatically become model features. Keep impression_id to identify the event; do not blindly feed a unique event identifier into the neural network.

CHAPTER 03

Turning feature values into model inputs

Categorical features identify things

User IDs, item IDs, categories, and device types are usually categorical. Their numerical spelling does not imply numerical distance: item 100 is not “twice” item 50.

A vocabulary maps each category to an integer index. An embedding table then maps each index to a small vector of learned numbers. Here is an invented mapping:

category vocabulary
PAD     -> 0
UNKNOWN -> 1
shoes   -> 2
books   -> 3
cameras -> 4

Illustrative learned embedding for shoes:
2 -> [0.12, -0.40, 0.08, 0.31]

The vector is a model parameter, learned during training. You do not manually write “0.12” into every raw shoes record. Raw records store the category; encoding produces an index; the model looks up its vector.

Each feature normally has its own vocabulary and embedding table. User index 2 and category index 2 are unrelated. A candidate item and a history item often share both a vocabulary and an embedding table. Shared indices alone do not ensure shared vectors: separate embedding tables can learn different vectors for the same index.

Reserve a way to represent unseen values, often called unknown or out of vocabulary. A new item can have an unknown item ID while still supplying useful category, price, and content features.

For very large vocabularies, feature hashing maps values into a fixed number of buckets. It saves vocabulary management but permits collisions: different values may share a bucket.

Numerical features measure quantities

Price, recent impression count, elapsed time, and video duration are numerical. They generally become floating-point values.

Possible transformations include dividing by a scale, standardizing using a training-set mean and standard deviation, or applying log(1+x) to a nonnegative count. Choose transformations for the feature's meaning; there is no mandatory universal normalization.

Missing and zero are different facts. “Price unavailable” is not the same as “free.” You can use a default value plus a separate missing-value indicator.

History features contain lists

A user's recent interactions form a variable-length list. A model batch (a group of examples processed together) often pads lists to a maximum length and supplies a length or mask identifying the real entries:

Actual history:        [A12, A18, A33]
Encoded and padded:   [ 12,  18,  33, 0, 0]
Valid-entry mask:     [  1,   1,   1, 0, 0]
Length:               3

Here the latest L=5 events are kept, ordered oldest first, and padded on the right. L is the maximum retained history length. Zero is reserved for padding; it cannot identify a normal item. The mask marks valid entries: 1/0 and True/False are two common representations.

If you include item IDs, categories, actions, and timestamps for each event, keep their positions aligned. The second category must describe the second item. For a first implementation, retain the latest L events in a documented order.

Providing an ordered list does not by itself make a model order-sensitive. A simple sum or average discards ordering. The Deep Interest Network (DIN) model, introduced later, weights historical behaviors by relevance to the candidate. Its weighted sum also discards order unless order-related features are added. Other sequence models can use positions or timestamps; a recurrent model updates a running summary as it processes each event.

Text and images are optional inputs

An item's title can become text tokens or a vector from a text encoder. An image can become pixels or a vector from an image encoder. These complement IDs, especially for unfamiliar items. They are not required to understand or train a basic CTR model.

TensorFlow's feature preprocessing tutorial provides concrete examples of processing IDs, numerical values, and text. Keep the same preprocessing definitions for training and live predictions; an index must mean the same thing in both places.

CHAPTER 04

A complete worked example

A human readable training record

The following JSON is an invented teaching schema for imp_101. It makes the feature boundary explicit.

{
  "metadata": {
    "impression_id": "imp_101",
    "request_id": "req_10",
    "prediction_time": "2026-11-01T09:59:58Z",
    "shown_at": "2026-11-01T10:00:00Z",
    "label_finalized_at": "2026-11-01T10:35:00Z"
  },
  "features": {
    "user_id": "U7",
    "candidate_item_id": "A42",
    "candidate_category": "shoes",
    "candidate_price": 80.0,
    "device": "mobile",
    "surface": "home_feed",
    "hour_utc": 9,
    "recent_history": [
      {"item_id": "A12", "category": "shoes"},
      {"item_id": "A18", "category": "shoes"},
      {"item_id": "A33", "category": "books"}
    ]
  },
  "labels": {
    "clicked": 1
  },
  "sample_weight": 1.0
}

metadata helps reconstruct and audit an example. features is the allowed prediction input. labels provides the target only during training and evaluation. A sample_weight tells the loss how much that example counts; 1.0 means ordinary equal weighting.

Here, price means the product's price, not the advertiser's bid. The choice of fields is illustrative; it does not claim that every production ranker takes these inputs.

The corresponding numerical input

Use these invented vocabularies. In every vocabulary here, 0 is reserved for padding and 1 for unknown; real values use indices 2 or greater. The digit-like ID mappings below are explicitly chosen entries, not a general rule for converting IDs. No real item gets index 0 or 1. Non-history features do not need padding in practice; this example reserves the same slots for clarity.

Feature Mapping
user_id U7 → 7
candidate_item_id and history_item_ids A12 → 12, A18 → 18, A33 → 33, A42 → 42
device mobile → 2
surface home_feed → 2
category shoes → 2, books → 3

Divide price by 100 and hour_utc by 23. The hour comes from the scoring time, which is still 09:59:58, so its value is 9. The simple hour scaling is for teaching; local hour, categorical hours, or cyclic representations can better capture daily patterns. Dense below means the measured numerical features. Sparse conventionally describes categorical features whose full one-hot representation would be mostly zeros. A one-hot vector has one position per vocabulary entry: 1 for the observed value and 0 everywhere else. With a million items, that is 999,999 zeros, so the model usually receives the compact index instead.

# Batch size B = 1; maximum history length L = 5.
x = {
    "user_id": [7],
    "candidate_item_id": [42],
    "candidate_category": [2],
    "device": [2],
    "surface": [2],
    "dense": [[0.80, 9 / 23]],
    "history_item_ids": [[12, 18, 33, 0, 0]],
    "history_category_ids": [[2, 2, 3, 0, 0]],
    "history_mask": [[True, True, True, False, False]]
}

y = [[1.0]]
weight = [[1.0]]

This Python dictionary describes tensor contents. A tensor is a numerical array with a shape and data type. A loader turns these lists into the arrays a framework expects.

Input Shape for batch size B Typical type
One categorical feature B or B × 1 Integer indices
Two numerical features B × 2 Float32
Item history B × 5 Integer indices
History mask B × 5 Boolean
Click label B × 1 Float32 for binary loss

For B=32, you stack 32 examples along the first dimension. That group is a batch. An epoch is one pass through the training dataset.

What the model does with it

A possible model looks up embeddings for the categorical values, summarizes the valid history entries, concatenates (joins end to end) the resulting vectors with the numerical features, and passes the result through a neural network. Its final output is a click probability.

For a binary label y and predicted probability p, binary cross-entropy is −[y × ln(p) + (1−y) × ln(1−p)]. Here ln is the natural logarithm; the formula makes a confident wrong prediction expensive. For p=0.20 and y=1, loss is −ln(0.20) ≈ 1.609. For y=0 it is −ln(0.80) ≈ 0.223. Log loss is this loss averaged over examples. Training adjusts parameters, including embeddings, to reduce it. The formula is conceptual; libraries use numerically stable implementations.

# Framework-neutral training outline, not runnable API code.
prediction = model(x)
loss_per_example = binary_cross_entropy(prediction, y)
loss = mean(weight * loss_per_example)
update_model_parameters(loss)

The pseudocode uses the mean of weighted losses. Some libraries divide by the sum of weights instead; this changes the scaling within a batch and can change the relative contribution of batches with different weight totals. Match your framework's reduction convention.

At prediction time, you have x but do not yet know y. To rank ten candidates, construct ten candidate-specific inputs. Some user and context computation can be shared across them.

CHAPTER 05

Published Criteo and DIN examples

Criteo provides real anonymized rows

The DeepCTR-Torch Criteo tutorial uses 13 numerical fields and 26 categorical fields. In its published sample file, the first example has label 0. These are selected fields from that exact row, not an invented record:

{
    "label": 0,
    "I1": None,
    "I2": 3,
    "I3": 260.0,
    "I5": 17668.0,
    "I8": 33.0,
    "C1": "05db9164",
    "C2": "08d6d899",
    "C3": "9143c832"
}

The original row has 39 feature columns, some empty; this excerpt omits the rest. The published feature names are anonymized. You cannot infer that C1 means user or that I3 means age.

The example training script replaces missing values, label-encodes categorical fields independently, and scales numerical columns. For the full 200-row sample, the first row's C1, C2, and C3 encode to 0, 4, and 96, respectively. These are vocabulary indices, not intrinsic meanings of the original strings.

The demo reserves no unknown index: zero can be a real category here, unlike our worked example. An unseen serving category needs an explicit handling rule. Filling missing numbers with zero also loses the distinction between missing and genuine zero unless an indicator is added. Public benchmark click rates can differ from live traffic; do not assume their probabilities transfer unchanged.

This example is good for understanding the mechanical path from table columns to embeddings. It is less useful for understanding the business meaning of each feature. NVIDIA's Criteo overview explains the anonymized numerical and hashed categorical format.

DIN makes candidate and history inputs explicit

Alibaba's DIN paper, Section 4.1, uses the feature example below, reformatted from a set of visited categories into a list:

{
    "weekday": "Friday",
    "gender": "Female",
    "visited_cate_ids": ["Bag", "Book"],
    "ad_cate_id": "Book"
}

The paper's idea is to build a user-interest representation that depends on which ad is being scored. A book candidate can emphasize book-related history.

For numerical input, the first toy example in DeepCTR-Torch's DIN demo is:

x = {
    "user": [0],
    "gender": [0],
    "item": [1],
    "item_gender": [1],
    "score": [0.1],
    "hist_item": [[1, 2, 3, 0]],
    "hist_item_gender": [[1, 1, 2, 0]],
    "seq_length": [3]
}
y = [1]

This is synthetic demonstration data from a third-party library, not an Alibaba production record. The history has three valid entries and one padding position. In this separate demo, zero is a real user or gender value but pads the item history; reserved indices are feature-specific and differ from our uniform teaching convention. The demo does not specify a business meaning for score. Candidate item 1 also occurs in its history: in real data that is valid only for a genuinely earlier interaction. The demo uses label shape B, while the worked example uses B × 1; match your library's required label shape and type.

Criteo and DIN illustrate different input structures. They are not two serializations of the same dataset.

CHAPTER 06

How data changes across recommendation tasks

“Recommendation training data” does not identify a single universal schema. First decide the question the model answers.

Task One example represents Target
CTR ranking One logged showing of a candidate Click within a defined window
Rating prediction A user rating an item A numerical rating
Retrieval A user or query context paired with a relevant item Relevant item versus contrasting items
Conversion prediction An eligible impression or click Attributed conversion within a window
Next-item prediction A history ending at a cutoff The next observed item
Pairwise ranking Two items under a shared context Which item is preferred
Listwise ranking A group of candidates under a shared request Per-item relevance or outcome labels

Ranking can train on individual rows

A model trained to predict clicks independently can still rank items by its predictions. It does not need to receive a sorted list during every training step. This is commonly called pointwise training.

For explicit ratings, a row might be user=U7, item=A42, rating=4. The rating is a numerical target, not a click label. TensorFlow's ranking tutorial demonstrates retaining the user, movie title, and rating, then predicting the rating.

Retrieval needs contrasting candidates

Retrieval finds a manageable candidate set from a large catalog. A common two-tower design separately turns user/context features and item features into vectors, then scores their compatibility.

An invented training example could be:

{
    "user_id": "U7",
    "history": ["A12", "A18"],
    "positive_item": "A42",
    "sampled_other_items": ["A81", "A90"]
}

Here a positive item is an observed relevant interaction, and a negative is a sampled contrast, not a proven dislike. Some training methods use other examples' positive items as in-batch negatives. You need not store every contrasting pair explicitly in the file. TensorFlow's retrieval tutorial demonstrates a two-tower setup with user-item interactions.

Popular items appear more often as other examples' positives, so the distribution of in-batch contrasts can be skewed. Some training methods adjust for their sampling probabilities.

A retrieval similarity score is not automatically a calibrated probability of a click. Also, an unobserved item may be relevant even when training uses it as a contrast.

Next-item prediction uses a shifted history

In an invented chronological history [A12, A18, A33, A42], one training example can be:

x = {"history": ["A12", "A18", "A33"]}
y = "A42"

The target must not appear in the input as a future event; earlier interactions with that same item are legitimate. In causal sequence training, each prediction sees only earlier positions; several positions can therefore supply targets. The target is an item identifier rather than a binary click.

Pairwise and listwise data preserve comparisons

Pairwise data might contain context, preferred_item, other_item. Listwise data might contain request_id, candidate_items, labels, valid_item_mask. Keep the request grouping so the loss knows which items are being compared. Padding a candidate list requires masking its padded entries.

Ads share input types but add business objectives

Ads can use the same user, item, context, and history inputs as product recommendations. They additionally involve payment rules, targeting, budgets, and advertiser objectives.

A conversion is a downstream action such as a purchase or signup. CPC means cost per click, a payment arrangement where a valid click is the billable event. A bid is the advertiser's offer per billable event. In a simplified CPC setup, a downstream scoring rule may multiply predicted click probability by a bid per click. The bid need not be a CTR model feature. Similarly, product price and advertiser bid are distinct quantities.

For conversion models, state the denominator. CVR means conversion rate; pCVR is a predicted conversion probability. Conditional probability means the chance of one event given specified information. A post-click model estimates P(conversion given click and impression features). An impression-level model estimates P(conversion given impression features).

For a common impression context x, the probability identity is:

P(click AND conversion | x)
  = P(click | x) × P(conversion | click, x)

The vertical bar means “given.” Thus pCTR × post-click pCVR estimates the joint click-and-conversion probability. It represents the probability of an attributed conversion per impression only if the conversion definition requires that matching click. It excludes view-through conversions, which are credited without a click. Click windows, invalid-click filtering, conversion windows, and attribution must agree. Any inputs needed at scoring must be available then; later post-click information cannot be silently used. A post-click CVR model trains on clicked rows but is applied to candidates whose click is not yet known. Extrapolating from this selected population is a form of sample selection bias. The joint prediction is sometimes written pCTCVR, meaning a predicted click-and-conversion probability.

Multiplying pCTR by an already impression-level conversion probability counts the click factor twice. When a probability is multiplied by bids or values, its calibration matters to the resulting economic score.

A multi-task record can carry click, conversion, and watch-time labels. Some targets are undefined for some rows; use explicit validity masks rather than silently treating every missing target as zero.

How attribution is done in practice

In the worked example, attribution was trivial: the click record carried the same impression_id as the impression. Conversions are harder. A purchase usually happens later, often on the advertiser's own website or app, and the person may have seen or clicked several ads first. Ad platforms solve this in three steps, and each step changes what your conversion label means:

  1. Link the conversion to earlier ad interactions.
  2. Filter those interactions by time windows.
  3. Assign credit when more than one interaction qualifies.

Step 1: Linking a conversion to ad interactions

The conversion and the ad interaction are logged by different systems, so something must connect them. The common mechanisms are:

Mechanism What connects the two events Documented example
Click identifier The ad platform adds a unique ID to the landing-page URL on each click. The advertiser stores it with the lead or order and sends it back with the conversion. Google's GCLID, used in offline conversion imports
Server event with customer information The advertiser's server sends the conversion with hashed customer details and any stored click ID. The platform matches them to its own users. Meta's Conversions API
On-device attribution The phone's operating system records ad impressions, decides the winner itself, and later sends the ad network a delayed report without a user identifier. Apple's AdAttributionKit

Concretely:

  • Google click identifier. With auto-tagging, Google adds a GCLID to each ad click's URL. The advertiser's page saves it, for example in a cookie, and attaches it to the lead record. When the lead later becomes a sale, the advertiser uploads the GCLID, the conversion name, and the conversion time. Depending on the import source, the click must be less than 14 or 90 days before the conversion.
  • Meta Conversions API. Contact fields such as email and phone must be SHA-256 hashed before sending. The click ID travels in the fbc value, which embeds the fbclid URL parameter. The same purchase often arrives twice, once from the browser pixel and once from the server. Meta deduplicates the pair when both carry the same event_id and event name and arrive within 48 hours of the first.
  • Apple AdAttributionKit. The device keeps qualifying impressions and picks one winning ad network after an install. Up to five other ad networks can receive a non-winning report. The winning network learns about the conversion through a postback, a signed report sent at least 24 to 48 hours after the event. Apple states that the postback contains no user- or device-specific data. It carries conversion values set by the advertised app, with less detail when too few people share the same values, a rule Apple calls crowd anonymity.

Chrome's Privacy Sandbox offered a browser-based equivalent, the Attribution Reporting API. Google announced its retirement on October 17, 2025.

Linking is never complete. A conversion without a stored click ID or matchable customer details cannot be attributed. In training data, such a row looks like "no attributed conversion" even though a sale happened.

Step 2: Windows decide which interactions qualify

A lookback window, also called a conversion window, is the period after an ad interaction during which a conversion can be credited to it. Windows are platform settings, not facts about users:

Platform Click-through View-through Other
Google Ads Default 30 days; 1 to 90 days depending on conversion source Default 1 day; up to 30 days Engaged-view for video: default 3 days
Meta 1 or 7 days after a link click 1 day after an impression Engage-through: 1 day after a non-link click or a 5-second video play
Apple AdAttributionKit 30 days from ad tap to install 24 hours from ad view to install First conversion value update within 60 days of install

Google states that a conversion after its window is not recorded, and a window change applies only to future conversions. If your label claims to match platform-reported conversions, it must use the same anchor, length, and interaction type.

Step 3: Credit rules when several interactions qualify

Suppose, in an invented journey, U7 clicks shoe ad A42 on November 1, sees a display ad for the same store on November 3 without clicking, clicks a search ad for the store on November 4, and buys on November 5. Both clicks fall inside a 30-day click-through window. The view happened two days before the purchase, so a 1-day view-through window excludes it. Different rules then divide the one conversion like this:

Rule A42 click (Nov 1) Display view (Nov 3) Search click (Nov 4)
Last click 0 0 (outside window) 1
First click 1 0 (outside window) 0
Linear 0.5 0 (outside window) 0.5
Data-driven Learned share 0 (outside window) Learned share

With a 3-day view-through window instead, the view would qualify, and linear credit would become one third each. The window and the credit rule interact.

  • Last click gives all credit to the last-clicked ad. Criteo's attribution paper calls last click within 30 days the industry standard; see Diemert et al., 2017.
  • Rules-based multi-touch models (first click, linear, time decay, and position-based) split credit by fixed formulas. Google's attribution models page says these four are no longer supported; conversion actions using them were upgraded to data-driven.
  • Data-driven attribution learns credit from data and is Google's default for most conversion actions. Google's description says it compares the paths of customers who convert to the paths of customers who do not, and recommends at least 200 conversions and 2,000 ad interactions in 30 days. A published academic basis for this family is the Shapley value from cooperative game theory, applied to advertising channels by Dalessandro et al., 2012, building on Shao and Li's 2011 KDD paper on data-driven multi-touch attribution.
  • Incremental attribution asks a different question: would this conversion have happened without the ad? Meta's standard attribution credits conversions within the chosen windows, while its incremental option optimizes for conversions that models predict were caused by the ad.

Counting is a separate setting. Google's counting options count either every conversion after an ad interaction or only one conversion per click.

Each platform attributes using only the interactions it can see and its own rules. Two platforms can therefore both claim the same purchase, and their totals need not add up to the advertiser's actual orders.

What this means for your training labels

Criteo's public Attribution Modeling for Bidding dataset shows the distinction in real data. Each of its 16.5 million rows is one impression with two separate targets. conversion is 1 if any conversion occurred in the 30 days after the impression, whether or not this impression was the last click. attribution is 1 only if the advertiser attributed that conversion to Criteo. Fields such as click_pos, click_nb, and time_since_last_click describe the click path.

When you build conversion labels:

  • Choose the target explicitly. "Any conversion within N days of this impression" and "conversion credited to this impression under rule R" are different labels with different rates.
  • Version the attribution definition. Record the linking method, windows, credit rule, and counting setting in the data dictionary. Platform defaults change over time, and mixing data from different rules changes what label 1 means.
  • Expect late and missing labels. Conversions can take place long after the impression; Chapelle, 2014 reports delays of up to a month in display advertising. Offline imports and on-device postbacks add reporting delay on top. Set label finalization after both the window and the reporting delay.
  • Treat fractional credit as a modeling decision. A data-driven share such as 0.4 is not an observed 0/1 outcome. If you train on it, document whether it is a regression target, a sample weight, or thresholded into a binary label.
  • Do not let attribution leak into features. A field such as click_pos or the final credited touchpoint is computed after the conversion. Keep it for labeling and analysis, not as a prediction input.

CHAPTER 07

Labels sampling and evaluation

A negative label needs an observation rule

A displayed item with no recorded click is evidence about that showing. It is not proof that the user dislikes the item. A candidate that was never displayed has no observed response to that opportunity.

For click training, keep impression logs as well as click logs. Click-only data cannot directly tell you the rate of clicks per impression.

Conversions may take hours or days. For an invented click-attributed conversion target measured over seven days from the impression, a record collected one hour after that impression cannot yet be confidently labeled “no conversion.” Wait for the window, mask immature labels, or use a method explicitly designed for delayed outcomes. Record the attribution definition, the window anchor, and when labels become final after allowing for delayed logs. A positive can be observed earlier, but retaining early positives alongside immature negatives can itself bias a training sample.

Sampling changes what the model sees

Suppose an invented dataset has 1,000 clicks and 99,000 non-clicks: the click rate is 1%. If you keep all clicks and only 1,000 non-clicks, the sampled rate becomes 50%.

A model trained without an appropriate adjustment may learn probabilities for the sampled population. A prediction of 50% would not mean a 50% click chance in live traffic.

If a row is retained with probability q, inverse-probability weighting uses weight 1/q. For this illustration, the retained negatives have weight 99 and positives weight 1. Other correction methods exist; whichever you choose must match the sampling procedure. Google's imbalanced dataset lesson discusses downsampling and compensating weights.

For honest probability evaluation, use an unsampled representative test set or appropriate evaluation weights. If negative sampling is independent of features within each class, AUC (a ranking metric measuring how often a random positive scores above a random negative, expanded in the metrics table below) is unchanged in expectation for fixed scores, but raw log loss and calibration on the sampled data are not population estimates.

Candidate sampling for retrieval serves a different purpose from discarding non-clicked impressions in CTR training. Keep those two choices distinct.

Evaluate predictions on later data

A useful initial split is older events for training, a later interval for validation, and a still later interval for a final test. These intervals are not themselves model features. They determine which examples are used for learning, choosing settings, and assessing the chosen model.

For conversion labels, make sure the training outcomes would have matured by the simulated model-build time, or explicitly account for their availability. A chronological split alone does not solve delayed-label leakage.

Fit vocabularies, scaling statistics, and other learned preprocessing on the training portion, then apply them consistently to validation, test, and serving inputs. Reserve unknown categories. The Criteo demo fits transformations before a random split; that is convenient demo code, not the evaluation procedure to copy for a temporal production problem.

The same user can legitimately appear in training and later test data if predicting returning users is your use case. To measure performance on new users or new items, construct that evaluation separately.

Match metrics to the target

Metric What it helps you inspect
Log loss Whether predicted probabilities agree with outcomes
AUC Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; measures how often a positive scores above a negative, counting ties as half
Calibration Whether groups predicted near 3% actually click near 3%
Recall at K Of all relevant items, the fraction appearing in the first K results; K is the list length
NDCG at K Normalized discounted cumulative gain; rewards relevance near the top, relative to an ideal ordering

For rare clicks, accuracy can be misleading: predicting “no click” for everything can appear very accurate.

Offline evaluation still reflects the old system's exposure choices. Items it rarely showed have little outcome data. Position, selection, and feedback loops can therefore bias results. An online experiment, often an A/B test, assigns live traffic to alternative systems to compare outcomes. Such experiments help measure a changed system's effect on users and the marketplace. Google's View from the Trenches is a useful follow-up on calibration and practical CTR evaluation.

CHAPTER 08

A practical starting schema

For a first CTR dataset, use one row per impression. Start with user, item, context, and a click label; add behavior lists when the simple path is understood.

Field Role Meaning
impression_id Metadata Unique showing identifier for joins and deduplication
request_id Metadata Groups items from one recommendation request
prediction_time Metadata Scoring decision time; defines the feature cutoff
shown_at Metadata Logged exposure time; anchors this guide's label windows
user_id Feature User identity, with an unknown value supported
candidate_item_id Feature Candidate identity, with an unknown value supported
candidate_category Feature Candidate category
device Feature Device class known when scoring
surface Feature Page or placement being scored
hour_utc Feature UTC hour derived from prediction_time
candidate_price Optional feature Product price as known at prediction time
recent_history Optional feature Aligned item and category records before the cutoff
history_length Input helper Number of valid history entries
clicked Label Attributed click within the defined window
label_finalized_at Metadata Time after which the click target is complete
sample_probability Metadata Probability that this example was retained
sample_weight Loss input Weight appropriate to the training procedure

Apply your organization's consent, access, and retention rules to user-level logs.

You can store this in Parquet, including list-valued history columns. CSV is convenient for the flat version; JSON is easier to inspect manually. A training loader reads records and produces the same logical numerical arrays regardless of storage format.

The loader turns recent_history into history_item_ids and history_category_ids, generates a mask, derives hour_utc from prediction_time, and puts transformed candidate_price and hour_utc into dense. It maps each categorical field (user, item, category, device, and surface) to indices. The JSON and the tensor dictionary therefore use different names only for explicit transformations.

Keep a small data dictionary beside the dataset. For each field, specify its meaning, type, allowed values, units, missing-value behavior, and whether it is an input or label. Also preserve the vocabulary, transformations, history order, maximum history length, target window, and schema version with the model.

Before training, inspect a few complete examples manually:

  1. Can you trace each label to a real impression and its attributed response?

  2. Do all features obey the decision-time cutoff?

  3. Are duplicated events removed without collapsing legitimate repeated impressions?

  4. Do padding, unknown, and missing values have distinct documented meanings?

  5. Are parallel history arrays aligned and lengths correct?

  6. Are training and live prediction encodings identical?

  7. Does the train/test split match the future behavior you want to evaluate?

Do not automatically feed every logged field into the model. For example, the actual final position after ranking may be unavailable when scoring candidates. Keep it for analysis; if a model uses position, define how it will know the proposed position during serving.

A successful first milestone is being able to select one raw impression and explain every number in its model input, every historical event included, and exactly why its label is 0 or 1.

CHAPTER 09

Sources and next steps

The published samples and the invented worked example serve different purposes. Use the original files when reproducing their exact preprocessing; use the worked example to understand the meaning of the fields.

Read Focus

For your first exercise, inspect a few rows of the Criteo sample and follow the numerical and categorical transformations in its script. Then inspect the DIN demo and identify the candidate, valid history entries, padding, and label. After that, build the invented impression example above in a small dataset of your own.

You understand the format when you can answer: What opportunity does this row describe? What was known at prediction time? What is being predicted? How did each field become a tensor? Which outcome supplied the label?

REFERENCE

Glossary and self check

Every technical term in the guide, explained so you do not need to look anything up elsewhere. Each entry starts with a one-line definition, then explains why it matters, works through a concrete example (mostly the same U7 / A42 impression used in the chapters), flags common mistakes, and links to related terms.

A/B testEvaluation

An online experiment that randomly splits live traffic between a current system (A) and a changed system (B) and compares what happens.

Offline metrics only tell you how a model scores old logged data. An A/B test answers the question that actually matters: when real people use the new system, do outcomes such as clicks, purchases, revenue, or satisfaction change? Traffic is randomly assigned so that the two groups are comparable, and the difference between groups is attributed to the change. The unit that gets randomized (a request, a user, an advertiser) must be chosen carefully: in an ads marketplace, changes to one group can affect budgets and prices seen by the other.

Example Half of users keep the current CTR model and half get a new one for two weeks. If the new group's clicks per impression rise from 2.0% to 2.1% and the difference is statistically reliable, the change is credited to the new model.

Watch out Randomizing by request lets the same user see both systems, so their experiences contaminate each other. Randomizing by user is often safer, and shared budgets can still leak effects between groups.

See also: Online experiment, Offline evaluation, Marketplace, Feedback loop

AccuracyEvaluation

The fraction of predictions that are correct after turning each probability into a yes/no decision with a threshold.

Accuracy is the share of examples where the predicted class matches the label. For rare outcomes like clicks it is almost useless, because always predicting 'no click' scores very well while learning nothing. Click models are judged with probability and ranking metrics instead, such as log loss, calibration, and AUC.

Example If 1% of impressions are clicked, a model that predicts 'no click' for every impression is 99% accurate and completely useless for ranking ads.

See also: Log loss, AUC, Calibration, Negative example

AdvertiserAds and business

The business that pays to have its ad shown, and that sets the bids, budgets, targeting, and goals for its campaigns.

In ads systems the item being ranked is an ad, and the advertiser behind it is a customer of the platform. Advertisers choose what they pay for (clicks, impressions, or conversions), how much they offer (the bid), how much they can spend (the budget), and whom they want to reach (targeting). These business settings shape which ads are eligible and how predicted probabilities are turned into money.

Example A shoe store runs ad A42 and offers $0.50 per click with a $100 daily budget, targeted at mobile users.

See also: Bid, Budget, Targeting, CPC, Conversion

Anonymized featureFeatures and encoding

A feature whose name and raw values have been replaced so that outsiders cannot tell what it originally measured or identified.

Public datasets often hide real field names and values to protect users and business secrets. Column names become generic labels such as I1 or C1, and category values become meaningless strings, often produced by hashing. You can still train a model on them because the model only needs consistent values, but you lose the ability to reason about what each feature means.

Example In the Criteo sample, column C1 has the value '05db9164'. You cannot tell whether C1 is a website, an advertiser, or a device; you only know equal strings mean the same original value.

Watch out Do not guess meanings from anonymized names or values. I3 is not 'age' just because it looks like a small number.

See also: Criteo dataset, Feature hashing, Categorical feature

AttentionModels and training

A mechanism that gives each item in a list a learned importance weight, based on how relevant it is to something else, and then takes the weighted sum.

A plain average treats every past behavior as equally important. Attention instead computes a relevance score between each history item and a query, here usually the candidate being scored, then combines the history using those scores as weights. The weights are produced by the model itself and are learned during training. DIN uses an attention-style unit so that a user's representation depends on which ad is being considered; its paper deliberately does not force the weights to add up to 1.

Example When scoring a shoe ad for U7, an attention unit might give the two shoe views weights 0.9 and 0.8 and the book view 0.1, so the summary looks mostly like 'interested in shoes'.

Watch out A weighted sum ignores order. Attention by itself does not know which event came first unless position or time features are added.

See also: DIN, Weighted sum, Pooling, History, Sequence model

AttributionLogs and joins

The rule that decides which earlier impression or click gets credit for a later outcome such as a click or purchase, and within what time window.

Outcomes are logged separately from the impressions that may have caused them, so something has to connect them. An attribution rule states which events are eligible (for example, only clicks on the same impression), how long after the impression an outcome still counts, and what happens when several impressions could claim the same outcome. The label of every training row depends on this rule, so it must be written down and applied the same way everywhere. In ads, conversions usually happen later on the advertiser's own site or app, so platforms first link the conversion to ad interactions (click identifiers, server events with hashed customer details, or on-device reports), then keep only interactions inside lookback windows, then split credit with a rule such as last click or data-driven.

Example Rule: a click counts for an impression if it carries the same impression_id and arrives within 30 minutes of shown_at. The click at 10:00:05 on imp_101 qualifies, so imp_101 gets label 1.

Watch out Matching outcomes only by user_id and item_id can credit one click to several separate showings of the same ad.

See also: Window, Click identifier, Last-click attribution, Data-driven attribution, View-through conversion, Label

AUCEvaluation

Area under the ROC curve: the probability that a randomly chosen positive example gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative example, with ties counting as half.

AUC measures ranking quality only: whether positives tend to be scored above negatives. It ranges from 0 to 1; 0.5 means no better than random ordering and 1.0 means every positive outranks every negative. Because it ignores the actual probability values, a model can have excellent AUC and still be badly calibrated, for example predicting 50% when the true rate is 1%. Click models usually report AUC alongside log loss and calibration.

Example Two positives scored 0.9 and 0.4, two negatives scored 0.5 and 0.1. Of the 4 positive-negative pairs, 3 have the positive on top (0.9>0.5, 0.9>0.1, 0.4>0.1) and 1 does not (0.4<0.5), so AUC = 3/4 = 0.75.

Watch out Multiplying every score by the same factor leaves AUC unchanged, so a good AUC says nothing about whether 0.03 really means 3%.

See also: ROC curve, Calibration, Log loss, Downsampling

AuctionAds and business

The process that decides which competing ads are shown for a request, and often what each winner pays, using bids combined with predicted outcomes.

When several advertisers want the same slot, the system ranks their ads by a score. In a simple cost-per-click setup the score is often the expected value per impression, roughly predicted click probability times bid. The pricing rule (for example, paying just enough to beat the next ad) is separate from ranking. Because predicted probabilities directly multiply money, poorly calibrated predictions distort who wins and what they pay.

Example Ad A42 bids $0.50 with pCTR 0.03, worth about $0.015 per impression. Ad A81 bids $1.00 with pCTR 0.01, worth $0.010. A42 ranks first despite the lower bid.

See also: Bid, eCPM, CPC, pCTR, Calibration, Marketplace

Available timeLogs and joins

The moment an event or feature value actually reached the system and could be used for scoring, which can be later than when the event happened.

Logs travel through queues and pipelines before they can be read, so every event has two times: when it occurred and when it became usable. A feature may only use events that were already available before the prediction time. Building training data with occurrence time alone quietly uses information that the live system did not yet have.

Example U7 views an item at 09:59:00, but the log reaches the feature store at 10:02. For the request scored at 09:59:58, that view must be excluded from the history even though it happened earlier.

Watch out Recording only occurred_at makes this check impossible later. Store available_at, or a known delay, alongside each event.

See also: Prediction time, Point-in-time join, Data leakage, Timestamp, Cutoff

BatchTensors and arrays

A group of training examples stacked together and processed in one step; B denotes how many examples are in it.

Computing on one example at a time wastes hardware, so training loaders stack many examples into arrays whose first dimension is B. The model produces B predictions at once, the losses are combined into one number, and the parameters are updated once per batch. Variable-length inputs such as histories must be padded to the same length to fit in one array.

Example With B = 32 and a history length of 5, history_item_ids is a 32 × 5 array of integers: one row per example.

See also: Shape, Tensor, Padding, Epoch, Data loader, In-batch negative

Benchmark datasetData formats

A public dataset that many researchers use so that models and methods can be compared on the same data.

Benchmarks make experiments reproducible and comparable, but they are snapshots from a particular platform and time, often sampled and anonymized. Their click rates, feature sets, and distributions can differ greatly from your traffic. Use them to learn mechanics and compare methods, not to assume a model's probabilities transfer to your system.

Example Criteo click logs are a common CTR benchmark. A model reaching a certain log loss on Criteo does not tell you its log loss on your shopping app.

See also: Criteo dataset, Anonymized feature, Calibration

BidAds and business

The amount an advertiser offers to pay for one billable event, such as one click.

The bid is set by the advertiser, not predicted by the model. Ranking systems usually combine the bid with a predicted probability of the billable event to estimate expected value per impression. Because the bid is used after prediction, it need not be a CTR feature. It is unrelated to the price of the advertised product.

Example A shoe store bids $0.50 per click on ad A42. The product itself costs $80; that is the candidate_price feature, not the bid.

Watch out Do not confuse bid with product price. They are different numbers with different owners and meanings.

See also: CPC, Auction, eCPM, Advertiser, pCTR

Binary cross-entropyModels and training

The standard loss for yes/no labels: −[y·ln(p) + (1−y)·ln(1−p)], where y is the 0/1 label and p the predicted probability.

Only one of the two terms is active for each example. If y = 1 the loss is −ln(p), small when p is near 1 and huge when p is near 0. If y = 0 the loss is −ln(1−p). The result is that confident wrong predictions are punished heavily, while correct confident predictions cost almost nothing. Averaged over examples it is called log loss. Libraries compute it in a numerically stable form rather than literally taking ln of a probability.

Example With p = 0.20: if the impression was clicked (y=1) the loss is −ln(0.20) ≈ 1.609; if not clicked (y=0) it is −ln(0.80) ≈ 0.223.

See also: Log loss, Loss, Natural logarithm, Sigmoid, Label, Numerical stability

BooleanMath and notation

A value that is either true or false, often stored as True/False or as 1/0.

Booleans are used for yes/no facts, and especially for masks that mark which positions in an array are real. Different libraries expect different encodings: some want a boolean type, others want 0.0/1.0 floats that can be multiplied directly into a loss.

Example history_mask = [True, True, True, False, False] says the first three history slots are real events and the last two are padding.

See also: Mask, Label mask, Tensor

BudgetAds and business

The maximum amount an advertiser is willing to spend over a period, such as a day or a whole campaign.

When a budget runs out, the advertiser's ads stop being eligible, which changes which ads appear for everyone else. Systems often pace spending so a daily budget lasts the whole day. Budgets are one reason ads experiments are tricky: changing one group's model can drain shared budgets and affect another group.

Example The shoe store has a $100 daily budget at $0.50 per click, so after about 200 billed clicks ad A42 stops serving until the next day.

See also: Advertiser, Bid, Marketplace, A/B test

CalibrationEvaluation

How well predicted probabilities match observed frequencies: among predictions near 3%, about 3% should actually happen.

A calibrated model's numbers can be read literally as probabilities. Check it by grouping predictions into ranges and comparing the average prediction in each range with the observed rate. Calibration matters most when probabilities are multiplied by money, as in ads auctions. It must be measured on the population where the model is used: training on downsampled data shifts predictions upward unless corrected.

Example Of 10,000 impressions scored around 0.03, roughly 300 should be clicked. If 600 are clicked, the model underpredicts by about 2×.

Watch out A model can rank perfectly (high AUC) and still be badly calibrated. Check both.

See also: AUC, Log loss, Downsampling, Inverse-probability weighting, eCPM

CandidateBasics

An item that is being considered for display on the current request but has not necessarily been shown.

Systems usually narrow a huge catalog to a few hundred or thousand candidates (retrieval), score each one (ranking), and show the top few. Every shown item was a candidate, but most candidates are never shown. Only shown items produce click labels.

Example For req_10, ads A42, A81, and A90 might be candidates. A42 and A81 were shown; A90 was not, so it has no click outcome for this request.

Watch out A candidate that was never shown is not a negative CTR example. Nobody had the chance to click it.

See also: Item, Retrieval, Ranking, Impression, Negative example

Categorical featureFeatures and encoding

A feature whose value names a category or entity, such as an item ID or device type, rather than measuring an amount.

Categories have no natural arithmetic: 'shoes' plus 'books' means nothing, and item ID 100 is not twice item ID 50. Models handle them by mapping each value to an integer index through a vocabulary and then looking up a learned embedding vector. Each categorical field normally has its own vocabulary.

Example device = 'mobile', surface = 'home_feed', and candidate_category = 'shoes' are categorical. In the worked example 'shoes' maps to index 2, which selects a learned vector.

See also: Vocabulary, Index, Embedding, Label encoding, Sparse feature, Dense feature

Causal sequence trainingRecommendation tasks

Training on a sequence where each position predicts the next event using only events that came before it, never later ones.

One user history can supply many training targets: predict event 2 from event 1, event 3 from events 1–2, and so on. A causal (left-to-right) mask makes sure each prediction cannot see the answer or any later event. This is efficient and mirrors what happens live, where future behavior is unknown.

Example From history [A12, A18, A33, A42]: predict A18 from [A12], A33 from [A12, A18], and A42 from [A12, A18, A33], all in one training pass.

See also: Next-item prediction, Sequence model, Mask, Data leakage

ClickBasics

A recorded interaction in which a person selects a displayed item, for example by tapping an ad.

Clicks are the most common label for ads and recommendation models because they are frequent and logged immediately. But not every logged click is valid: accidental taps, bots, and duplicate log entries are often filtered out. A training label needs an explicit rule saying which clicks count, how they are attributed to impressions, and how long after the impression they may occur.

Example A click on imp_101 is logged at 10:00:05, five seconds after it was shown at 10:00:00. It falls inside the 30-minute window, so imp_101 has label 1.

See also: Impression, CTR, Attribution, Invalid click, Deduplication, Window

Click identifierAds and business

A unique ID an ad platform adds to the landing-page URL when someone clicks an ad, so a later conversion can be linked back to that click.

The advertiser's site saves the ID, for example in a cookie, and stores it with the lead or order. When the conversion happens, possibly days later and outside the ad platform, the advertiser sends the ID back with the conversion time. The platform then finds the original click. Google calls its identifier the GCLID; Meta's click ID appears as the fbclid URL parameter and inside the fbc value.

Example U7 clicks a search ad and lands on the store's page with a GCLID in the URL. The page saves it; when U7's lead becomes a sale, the store uploads that GCLID with the sale time and Google credits the click.

Watch out If the landing page drops the ID, or the user declines storage, the conversion cannot be linked. It then looks like 'no attributed conversion' even though a sale happened.

See also: Attribution, Server-side conversion event, Join, Identifier

Cold startFeatures and encoding

The problem of making good predictions for new users or new items that have little or no interaction history.

A brand-new item has no learned ID embedding, or an embedding barely trained, because it rarely appeared in training data. Systems cope by relying on features that exist from day one, such as category, price, title text, or images, and by reserving an unknown index for unseen IDs. Evaluation for new users or items should be built separately, because averages over mostly familiar users hide cold-start performance.

Example A new shoe A99 launches today. Its item ID maps to the unknown index, but its category 'shoes' and price $70 still give the model useful signal.

See also: Out of vocabulary, Content feature, Embedding, Reserved index

CollisionFeatures and encoding

When feature hashing maps two different original values to the same bucket, so the model cannot tell them apart.

Hashing squeezes an unlimited set of values into a fixed number of buckets. With fewer buckets than values, some values must share. Colliding values share one embedding row, so whatever the model learns for one also affects the other. More buckets reduce collisions at the cost of memory.

Example With 1,000 buckets, item IDs 'A42' and 'Z9001' might both hash to bucket 517 and be treated as the same item.

See also: Feature hashing, Embedding table, Vocabulary

ConcatenateMath and notation

Join several vectors end to end into one longer vector.

Models commonly look up an embedding for each categorical feature, summarize the history into a vector, then concatenate everything with the numerical features into a single input for the next layers. The order of pieces must be fixed and identical in training and serving.

Example Concatenating [0.1, 0.2] (user embedding), [0.5, −0.3] (item embedding), and [0.80, 0.39] (dense features) gives [0.1, 0.2, 0.5, −0.3, 0.80, 0.39].

See also: Vector, Embedding, Dense feature, Neural network

Conditional probabilityMath and notation

The probability of one event given that certain information is known, written P(A | B) and read 'probability of A given B'.

Conditioning changes the population you are talking about. P(conversion | click) is measured only among clicked impressions; P(conversion) among all impressions. Ads models must say what they condition on, because multiplying the wrong conditional probabilities double-counts or mixes populations.

Example If 2% of impressions are clicked and 5% of clicks lead to a purchase, then P(click) = 0.02, P(purchase | click) = 0.05, and P(click and purchase) = 0.02 × 0.05 = 0.001.

See also: Joint probability, Probability, pCVR, Post-click model, pCTCVR

Content featureFeatures and encoding

A feature describing what an item is (its category, price, title text, or image) rather than its identity.

ID features let a model memorize facts about specific items, but they only work for items seen often in training. Content features generalize: a new item with a familiar category, similar title, or similar image can borrow what the model learned from related items. Text and images are usually converted to vectors by an encoder first.

Example Ad A42's category 'shoes', price $80, and the title 'Lightweight running shoe' are content features. Its ID 'A42' is not.

See also: Cold start, Encoder, Categorical feature, Item

ContextBasics

Information about the current situation in which something might be shown, such as device, page, time, and search query.

The same user might respond differently on a phone at breakfast than on a laptop at night. Context features capture the circumstances of the request rather than the user or item themselves. They must be known at prediction time.

Example For req_10 the context is device = mobile, surface = home_feed, and hour_utc = 9.

See also: Request, Surface, Feature, Prediction time

ConversionAds and business

A valuable downstream action, such as a purchase, signup, or app install, that an advertiser ultimately cares about.

Conversions happen after clicks, often hours or days later, and often on another website or app. They are rarer and more delayed than clicks, so labels take longer to become final. A conversion label must state exactly which action counts, which impression or click it is attributed to, and the time window.

Example U7 clicks ad A42 at 10:00:05 and buys the shoes at 18:30 the same day. Under a 7-day click-attributed rule, imp_101 has conversion label 1.

See also: CVR, pCVR, Attribution, Delayed feedback, View-through conversion, CPA

CPAAds and business

Cost per action (or acquisition): a payment arrangement in which the advertiser pays when a defined conversion happens.

Under CPA, the billable event is a conversion, so the platform needs good conversion predictions to estimate the expected value of showing an ad. Conversion labels are delayed and attribution-dependent, which makes CPA models harder to train and evaluate than click models.

Example An app pays $5 per install. If pCTR = 0.02 and post-click install probability = 0.10, the expected value per impression is 0.02 × 0.10 × $5 = $0.01.

See also: Conversion, CPC, CPM, pCVR, Bid

CPCAds and business

Cost per click: a payment arrangement in which the advertiser pays each time a valid click occurs.

With CPC billing the platform earns nothing from an impression that is not clicked, so it estimates the value of an impression as roughly pCTR × bid. This is why click prediction is central to ads and why calibration matters: an overestimated pCTR inflates an ad's apparent value.

Example A $0.50 CPC bid with pCTR 0.03 gives an expected $0.015 per impression.

See also: Bid, pCTR, eCPM, CPM, CPA, Invalid click

CPMAds and business

Cost per mille: a payment arrangement in which the advertiser pays per thousand impressions, regardless of clicks.

'Mille' is Latin for thousand. CPM billing is common for brand-awareness campaigns. It also provides a common unit for comparing ads billed in different ways: converting every ad's expected value to a per-thousand-impressions figure gives eCPM.

Example A $4 CPM means the advertiser pays $4 for every 1,000 impressions, or $0.004 per impression.

See also: eCPM, CPC, CPA, Impression

Criteo datasetData formats

A widely used public click-log dataset from the ad company Criteo, with a 0/1 click label, 13 numerical columns, and 26 anonymized categorical columns.

Each row describes one ad impression and whether it was clicked. Numerical columns are named I1–I13 and categorical columns C1–C26; categorical values are hashed strings, and many cells are empty. Full releases are very large; this guide uses a small 200-row sample distributed with the DeepCTR-Torch library to show how columns become model inputs.

Example The first sample row has label 0, I1 missing, I2 = 3, I3 = 260.0, and C1 = '05db9164'.

Watch out The feature meanings are hidden, and its click rate need not match your traffic. Use it to learn mechanics, not business meaning.

See also: Benchmark dataset, Anonymized feature, Label encoding, Missing value, CTR

CSVData formats

Comma-separated values: a plain-text table where each line is a row and commas separate the columns.

CSV is simple and readable, but it stores everything as text and has no built-in types. The reader has to guess or be told whether a column is a number, a string, or a date. That guessing causes bugs: IDs lose leading zeros, empty cells become 0 or empty strings, and list-valued columns need custom encoding.

Example impression_id,user_id,item_id,clicked
imp_101,U7,A42,1
imp_102,U7,A81,0

Watch out An ID like '007' read as a number becomes 7, and may now collide with another ID. Read ID columns as strings.

See also: JSON, Parquet, Schema, Missing value

CTRBasics

Click-through rate: the fraction of eligible impressions that received at least one valid, attributed click.

CTR is the base rate the click model tries to predict for each individual impression. In this guide each impression contributes a binary label, so multiple clicks on the same showing still count once. Typical ad CTRs are small, often around a few percent or less, which is why accuracy is a poor metric and why sampling must be handled carefully.

Example If 1,000 impressions produce 20 impressions with at least one valid click, CTR = 20 / 1,000 = 2%.

Watch out Using clicks / impressions with raw click counts (including repeats) gives a different number. State which definition you use.

See also: pCTR, Click, Impression, Denominator, Label

CutoffLogs and joins

The moment that separates information a feature may use (before) from information it may not use (after); normally the prediction time.

Every feature in a training row must be computed as if you were standing at the cutoff and could not see the future. Events after the cutoff can only be used to build the label. Getting this boundary wrong is the most common source of data leakage.

Example For imp_101 the cutoff is 09:59:58. U7's views at 09:40, 09:50, and 09:55 are allowed in the history; the click at 10:00:05 is not.

See also: Prediction time, Point-in-time join, Data leakage, Available time

CVRAds and business

Conversion rate: conversions divided by a stated population, such as clicks or impressions.

Unlike CTR, CVR has no single standard denominator. Post-click CVR divides by clicked impressions; impression-level CVR divides by all impressions. These differ by a factor of the CTR, so always state which one you mean.

Example 1,000 impressions, 20 clicks, 2 purchases. Post-click CVR = 2/20 = 10%. Impression-level CVR = 2/1,000 = 0.2%.

See also: Conversion, pCVR, Denominator, Conditional probability

Cyclic encodingFeatures and encoding

Representing a repeating quantity, such as hour of day, with sine and cosine so that the end of the cycle sits next to the beginning.

If hour is scaled as hour/23, then 23:00 (1.0) and 00:00 (0.0) look as far apart as possible, although they are one hour apart. Mapping the hour to a point on a circle with sin(2π·h/24) and cos(2π·h/24) fixes this. Treating each hour as a category is another option.

Example Hour 9 becomes (sin(2π·9/24), cos(2π·9/24)) ≈ (0.707, −0.707). Hours 23 and 0 become (−0.259, 0.966) and (0, 1), which are close.

See also: Normalization, Dense feature, Categorical feature

Data dictionaryData formats

A document listing every field in a dataset with its meaning, type, units, allowed values, missing-value handling, and role.

Without a data dictionary, the meaning of a dataset lives in someone's head. Writing it down means anyone can tell what each column is, whether it is a feature, label, or metadata, and how it was computed. It should also record dataset-wide choices: vocabularies, transformations, history order and length, label windows, and the schema version.

Example candidate_price: product price in USD as of prediction_time; float; ≥ 0; null if unknown, with a separate price_missing flag; role = feature.

See also: Schema, Metadata, Feature, Label, Missing value

Data leakageLogs and joins

Training or evaluating with information the real system would not have at prediction time, often a piece of the answer itself.

Leakage makes offline results look excellent and then collapses in production, because the model has learned to rely on information that will not exist live. Common sources: including the outcome event in the history, computing counts as of the dataset build date instead of the prediction time, using a price that changed later, fitting preprocessing on the test set, or using labels that had not matured yet.

Example Putting U7's 10:00:05 click on A42 into the history used to predict that same click lets the model 'see' the answer.

Watch out Leakage is usually silent: no error, just suspiciously good metrics. Treat an unexpectedly huge improvement as a bug until proven otherwise.

See also: Cutoff, Point-in-time join, Available time, Fitting, Immature label

Data loaderTensors and arrays

The code that reads stored training records, applies encodings, and assembles them into batches of tensors for the model.

The loader is where human-readable records become numbers: it looks up vocabulary indices, scales numerical values, truncates and pads histories, builds masks, and stacks examples into a batch. Because serving needs the exact same transformations, loader logic should be shared with, or tested against, the serving code.

Example The loader reads imp_101's JSON record and produces history_item_ids = [[12, 18, 33, 0, 0]] and dense = [[0.80, 0.391]].

See also: Batch, Encoding, Preprocessing, Training-serving skew, Padding

Data-driven attributionAds and business

Multi-touch attribution where the credit split is learned from data rather than fixed by a formula.

Google describes its data-driven model as comparing the paths of customers who convert with the paths of those who do not, to estimate each interaction's contribution. It is Google's default for most conversion actions, and Google recommends at least 200 conversions and 2,000 ad interactions in 30 days. Academic work in this family uses the Shapley value to divide credit among channels.

Example Instead of 0.5 and 0.5, a data-driven model might give U7's earlier A42 click 0.3 and the later search click 0.7, because paths containing that search click convert much more often.

Watch out Fractional credit is an estimate, not an observed outcome. If you use it as a training target, document how.

See also: Multi-touch attribution, Shapley value, Last-click attribution, Attribution

DeduplicationLogs and joins

Removing extra copies of the same logged event, while keeping genuinely separate events that merely look alike.

Logging systems sometimes write the same event more than once, for example when a phone retries a request. Duplicates inflate counts and labels. Deduplicate using a unique event identifier, not by user and item, because the same user can legitimately see the same ad twice.

Example Two click records both carry impression_id imp_101 and the same clicked_at: they are one event. Two separate impressions of A42 to U7 with different impression_ids are two events.

Watch out Deduplicating on (user_id, item_id) erases real repeated showings and their outcomes.

See also: Identifier, Impression, Click, Join

Delayed feedbackLabels and sampling

The situation where an outcome can occur long after the impression, so recent examples do not yet have final labels.

Clicks usually happen within seconds, but conversions can take days. If you build training data too soon, many future converters look like non-converters. Options include waiting until the window closes, masking immature labels, or using methods designed for delayed outcomes.

Example With a 7-day conversion window, an impression from one hour ago with no purchase yet is not a negative. Its label is unknown for another 6 days and 23 hours.

See also: Immature label, Label finalization, Window, Conversion

DenominatorMath and notation

The number you divide by when computing a rate; it defines which population the rate describes.

Two rates with the same numerator can mean very different things if their denominators differ. Clicks per impression and conversions per click answer different questions. Always state the denominator explicitly, especially for conversion rates.

Example 2 conversions / 20 clicks = 10%, but 2 conversions / 1,000 impressions = 0.2%. Same numerator, different denominator.

See also: CTR, CVR, Conditional probability

Dense featureFeatures and encoding

In this guide, a numerical measurement fed to the model directly as a floating-point number, such as a scaled price.

Dense features measure quantities, so their size carries meaning: a price of 0.80 is lower than 1.20. They are usually scaled so values are in a comfortable range. More generally in computing, 'dense' means an array stored with every entry present, as opposed to 'sparse', where most entries are zero and are not stored.

Example dense = [[0.80, 9/23]] holds candidate_price / 100 and hour_utc / 23 for imp_101.

See also: Sparse feature, Normalization, Float32, Missing value

DimensionTensors and arrays

One axis of an array, or the number of entries along that axis; also used for the length of a vector.

A matrix has two dimensions (rows and columns). A batch of histories with shape B × 5 has a batch dimension of size B and a history dimension of size 5. 'Embedding dimension' means how many numbers are in each embedding vector.

Example An embedding table with 1,000,000 rows and 64 columns has embedding dimension 64.

See also: Shape, Tensor, Vector, Matrix

DINModels and training

Deep Interest Network: an Alibaba CTR model that weights each past behavior by how relevant it is to the ad being scored.

Before DIN, many models pooled a user's history into one fixed vector regardless of the candidate. DIN computes a relevance weight between the candidate and each history item with a small learned network, an attention-style unit, and takes the weighted sum. So the same user is represented differently for a book ad than for a shoe ad. The weighted sum by itself ignores order; position or time features are needed if order matters.

Example Scoring a book ad, DIN might weight U7's book view highly and the two shoe views lightly; scoring a shoe ad, the reverse.

See also: Attention, Weighted sum, History, Pooling, Embedding

Dot productMath and notation

Multiply the matching entries of two equal-length vectors and add up the products.

The dot product is a fast similarity score: it is large when two vectors point in similar directions and have large entries. Two-tower retrieval models score a user against millions of items with dot products because they can be computed efficiently at scale.

Example [1, 2] · [3, 4] = 1×3 + 2×4 = 11. A user vector [0.5, 1.0] and item vector [0.2, 0.4] give 0.1 + 0.4 = 0.5.

See also: Vector, Two-tower model, Score, Embedding

DownsamplingLabels and sampling

Deliberately keeping only a fraction of some examples, usually the plentiful negatives, to make training cheaper or more balanced.

With a 1% click rate, 99% of rows are negatives that each carry little information. Keeping only some of them saves storage and compute. But the model now sees a different click rate than reality, so its probabilities shift upward unless you correct with weights or a known adjustment.

Example Keep all 1,000 clicks but only 1,000 of 99,000 non-clicks. The sampled click rate becomes 50% instead of 1%.

Watch out Without correction, a downsampled model's 50% does not mean a 50% click chance in live traffic.

See also: Sample probability, Inverse-probability weighting, Sample weight, Calibration

eCPMAds and business

Effective cost per mille: an ad's expected value per thousand impressions, used to compare ads billed in different ways.

For a CPC ad, eCPM ≈ pCTR × bid × 1,000. For a CPA ad, eCPM ≈ pCTR × pCVR (given click) × bid × 1,000. Converting everything to this common unit lets an auction rank ads with different billing types. Since eCPM multiplies predicted probabilities directly, miscalibration changes rankings and prices.

Example pCTR 0.03 and a $0.50 CPC bid: 0.03 × 0.50 × 1,000 = $15 eCPM.

See also: CPM, CPC, CPA, Auction, Calibration

EmbeddingFeatures and encoding

A short list of learned numbers (a vector) that represents a category, such as an item, user, or device.
