The model cannot do arithmetic on 'shoes', so it gives each category a vector of, say, 16 or 64 numbers. These start random and are adjusted during training like any other parameter. Categories that behave similarly tend to end up with similar vectors. The raw dataset stores only the category; the vector lives inside the model.

Example After training, 'shoes' (index 2) might have the embedding [0.12, −0.40, 0.08, 0.31]. Nobody chose those numbers; training did.

See also: Embedding table, Vector, Index, Parameters, Categorical feature

Embedding tableFeatures and encoding

A learned matrix with one row per vocabulary index; looking up index i returns row i as that category's embedding.

Each categorical feature usually has its own table. A candidate item and history items often share one table, so the same item has the same vector in both places. Tables can be huge: they are often the largest part of an ads model.

Example 1,000,000 items × 64 numbers × 4 bytes (float32) ≈ 256 MB for a single item table.

Watch out Sharing a vocabulary does not by itself share a table. Two separate tables give index 42 two different vectors.

See also: Embedding, Vocabulary, Index, Matrix, Parameters

EncoderModels and training

A model or function that turns an input, such as text, an image, or an ID, into a vector of numbers.

Encoders let a recommender use rich content. A text encoder turns an item title into a vector; an image encoder turns a product photo into one. The vectors can be computed in advance by a separate model or learned jointly with the recommender.

Example A text encoder maps the title 'Lightweight running shoe' to a 384-number vector that sits close to vectors of other running-shoe titles.

See also: Content feature, Embedding, Token, Vector

EncodingFeatures and encoding

Converting raw feature values into the numbers the model receives, using a fixed, documented rule.

Each feature type has its own encoding: categories become vocabulary indices, prices become scaled floats, histories become padded index arrays with masks. The rules are part of the model: change them and old embeddings or weights stop meaning the same thing.

Example Encoding imp_101: device 'mobile' → 2; candidate_price 80.0 → 0.80; history [A12, A18, A33] → [12, 18, 33, 0, 0].

See also: Label encoding, Normalization, Padding, Preprocessing, Training-serving skew

Engaged-view conversionAds and business

A conversion credited to a video ad after the person watched a meaningful part of it without clicking.

Platforms define the engagement threshold and window themselves. Google Ads has an engaged-view window with a 3-day default. Meta's engage-through setting counts conversions within 1 day of a non-link click, or of a video play of at least 5 seconds (or 97% of a shorter video).

Example U7 watches 10 seconds of a shoe video ad, does not click, and buys the next day. Under a 1-day engage-through setting, the video ad gets credit.

See also: View-through conversion, Window, Attribution

EpochModels and training

One complete pass over the training dataset.

Training often runs for several epochs, with examples shuffled between passes. Large ads datasets may be trained for only one epoch, or continuously on fresh data, because new logs keep arriving and repeated passes can overfit ID embeddings.

Example A dataset of 3,200 examples with B = 32 takes 100 batches, or 100 parameter updates, per epoch.

See also: Batch, Training, Overfitting

EvaluationEvaluation

Measuring how well a trained model performs on data it did not learn from.

Scoring a model on its own training data is misleading, because it may have memorized those examples. Evaluation uses held-out data, ideally from a later time period, and metrics matched to the task. Offline evaluation uses logged data; online evaluation uses live experiments.

Example Train on Nov 1–20, tune settings on Nov 21–25, and report final metrics on Nov 26–30.

See also: Validation set, Test set, Temporal split, Offline evaluation, Online experiment

Explicit feedbackRecommendation tasks

A direct statement of preference from the user, such as a star rating, thumbs up, or 'not interested'.

Explicit feedback says clearly what the user thinks but is rare, because most people do not rate things. It also has its own biases: people tend to rate items they chose and felt strongly about. Compare implicit feedback, which is inferred from behavior.

Example U7 gives ad A42's product 4 stars: user=U7, item=A42, rating=4.

See also: Implicit feedback, Rating prediction, Label

FeatureBasics

A piece of information the model is allowed to use to make a prediction; all features together are written x.

Features describe the user, the candidate item, the context, and earlier behavior. A field qualifies as a feature only if its value would be known at prediction time and if using it is intended. Labels and bookkeeping fields such as event IDs are deliberately kept out.

Example For imp_101: user_id U7, candidate_item_id A42, category shoes, price 80.0, device mobile, surface home_feed, hour 9, and the three earlier views.

See also: Label, Metadata, Context, Categorical feature, Dense feature, Cutoff

Feature hashingFeatures and encoding

Mapping each value to an integer bucket with a hash function, bucket = hash(value) mod N, instead of keeping an explicit vocabulary.

A vocabulary must be built, stored, and updated as new values appear. Hashing skips that: any value, including one never seen before, gets a bucket instantly. The trade-off is collisions, since different values can land in the same bucket and share an embedding.

Example With N = 1,000,000 buckets, item 'A42' might go to bucket 381,207. A brand-new item tomorrow also gets a bucket without updating anything.

See also: Collision, Vocabulary, Out of vocabulary, Embedding table

Feedback loopEvaluation

The cycle in which a model decides what gets shown, those showings produce the data, and that data trains the next model.

Items the current model likes get shown and collect labels; items it dislikes rarely get shown, so the next model has little evidence to change its mind. Over time this can lock in early mistakes and favor already-popular items. Exploration (sometimes showing less certain items) and careful evaluation help counter it.

Example A new ad starts with low pCTR, so it is rarely shown, so it collects few clicks, so its pCTR stays low, whether or not people would actually like it.

See also: Selection bias, Position bias, Offline evaluation, Cold start

FittingModels and training

Learning values from data, either model parameters or preprocessing statistics such as a vocabulary, mean, or standard deviation.

Anything fitted must be fitted only on training data, then frozen and applied unchanged to validation, test, and serving data. Fitting a vocabulary or scaling statistics on all data, including the test period, leaks future information into evaluation.

Example Compute the mean price ($100) and standard deviation ($50) from November 1–20 training rows only, then use those same two numbers to scale every later row.

See also: Preprocessing, Standardization, Data leakage, Vocabulary

Float32Tensors and arrays

A 32-bit (4-byte) floating-point number type, the most common numerical type in model training.

Float32 stores about 7 significant decimal digits, which is plenty for features, labels, and most parameters, and it halves memory compared with 64-bit floats. Binary labels are usually stored as float32 (0.0 or 1.0) because the loss is computed with floating-point arithmetic.

Example 9/23 is stored in float32 as approximately 0.39130434.

See also: Floating-point number, Tensor, Integer

Floating-point numberMath and notation

A computer number that can have a fractional part, such as 0.80 or −3.5, stored with limited precision.

Floating-point numbers represent measurements, probabilities, and learned parameters. Their precision is finite, so tiny rounding errors occur; very small or very large values can underflow or overflow, which is why libraries use numerically stable formulas.

Example candidate_price / 100 = 0.80 and a predicted probability of 0.03 are floating-point values; vocabulary index 42 is an integer.

See also: Float32, Integer, Numerical stability

FrameworkModels and training

A software library for building and training models, such as PyTorch or TensorFlow.

Frameworks provide tensors, layers, loss functions, and automatic computation of the updates needed for training. Each framework and library has its own conventions for tensor shapes, data types, and how losses are averaged, so code and data must match the one you use.

Example DeepCTR-Torch is a recommendation library built on PyTorch; TensorFlow Recommenders is built on TensorFlow.

See also: Tensor, Reduction, Data loader, Neural network

Gradient descentModels and training

The basic training method: nudge each parameter a small step in the direction that reduces the loss.

For each parameter the framework computes the gradient: how much the loss would change if that parameter increased slightly. It then subtracts the gradient times a small step size called the learning rate. Repeating this over many batches gradually lowers the loss. In practice, variants that adapt the step size are common.

Example A weight is 0.5, its gradient is 2.0, and the learning rate is 0.1. The update gives 0.5 − 0.1 × 2.0 = 0.3.

See also: Training, Loss, Parameters, Batch, Hyperparameter

Half-open intervalMath and notation

A time or number range that includes its start but excludes its end, written [start, end).

Half-open intervals let consecutive ranges meet without overlapping or leaving gaps: [09:00, 10:00) and [10:00, 11:00) share no moment and miss none. Any label window or validity range must state which endpoints are included.

Example A click window [10:00:00, 10:30:00) counts a click at exactly 10:00:00 but not one at exactly 10:30:00.

See also: Window, Point-in-time join, Timestamp

HistoryFeatures and encoding

The list of a user's interactions that happened, and were available, before the prediction cutoff.

History is often the most predictive input: someone who just viewed three running shoes probably likes running shoes. Because it is a variable-length list, it must be truncated to a maximum length, ordered consistently, padded, and masked. Every event in it must pass the time check.

Example U7's history at 09:59:58: [A12 (shoes, view 09:40), A18 (shoes, view 09:50), A33 (books, view 09:55)].

Watch out The history must not contain the outcome being predicted, or any event after the cutoff.

See also: Truncation, Padding, Mask, Cutoff, Available time, DIN

HyperparameterModels and training

A setting chosen by people rather than learned by training, such as learning rate, embedding size, or history length.

Parameters are learned by gradient descent; hyperparameters control how that learning happens and how big the model is. They are chosen by trying several values and comparing results on the validation set, never on the test set.

Example Embedding dimension 64, batch size 32, maximum history length L = 5, and learning rate 0.001 are hyperparameters.

See also: Parameters, Validation set, Gradient descent

IdentifierLogs and joins

A value whose only job is to name one specific thing, such as an impression, request, user, or item.

Event identifiers like impression_id and request_id link tables, deduplicate events, and audit examples. Entity identifiers like user_id and item_id may also become categorical features. A unique per-event ID should not be fed to the model, because each value appears only once and carries no reusable pattern.

Example imp_101 identifies one showing; req_10 identifies the request that produced imp_101 and imp_102; U7 identifies a user.

See also: Join, Deduplication, Metadata, Categorical feature

Immature labelLabels and sampling

A label whose observation window has not finished yet, so its final value is still unknown.

A missing outcome during an open window means 'not yet', not 'no'. Treating immature examples as negatives teaches the model that recent impressions rarely convert. Exclude them, mask them, or use a delayed-feedback method.

Example At 10:20, imp_102 has no click, but its 30-minute window plus 5-minute log allowance runs until 10:35. Its label is immature until then.

See also: Label finalization, Delayed feedback, Label mask, Window

Implicit feedbackRecommendation tasks

Preference inferred from behavior, such as clicks, views, purchases, or watch time, rather than stated directly.

Implicit feedback is plentiful because it is logged automatically, but it is noisy. A click may be accidental and a non-click may mean the user simply did not notice the item. Most ads and recommendation training data is implicit.

Example U7 viewing three shoe pages suggests an interest in shoes, although U7 never said so.

See also: Explicit feedback, Click, Negative example, Watch time

ImpressionBasics

A logged showing of one item to one user at one time, under a stated definition of what counts as 'shown'.

The impression is the basic unit of a CTR dataset: one impression, one row, one 0/1 label. Systems define exposure differently (rendered on the page, visible for a minimum time, scrolled into view), and the definition changes the click rate. An impression record shows the item was displayed, not that the person looked at it.

Example imp_101: ad A42 shown to U7 on home_feed at 10:00:00, produced by request req_10.

See also: Click, CTR, Candidate, Request, Position bias

In-batch negativeRecommendation tasks

In retrieval training, using other examples' positive items in the same batch as contrasting candidates for the current example.

Retrieval models learn by scoring the true item above alternatives. Instead of storing sampled alternatives, a batch of B (user, positive item) pairs supplies B−1 free contrasts per user. Popular items appear more often as other users' positives, so they become over-represented contrasts; sampling-bias correction adjusts for that.

Example Batch: (U7, A42), (U9, A81), (U3, A90). For U7, A81 and A90 serve as negatives; for U9, A42 and A90 do.

Watch out An in-batch negative is not a known dislike. U7 might well like A81.

See also: Negative example, Retrieval, Two-tower model, Sampling bias correction, Batch

Incremental attributionAds and business

Crediting an ad only for conversions it is estimated to have caused, rather than every conversion that followed it within a window.

Window-based attribution credits a conversion that would have happened anyway, for example a loyal customer who was going to buy regardless. Incremental approaches try to estimate the causal effect. Meta offers an incremental attribution model that optimizes for conversions its models predict were caused by the ad.

Example U7 was already on the way to buy the shoes; an ad shown the same morning gets window-based credit but little incremental credit.

See also: Attribution, A/B test, Data-driven attribution

IndexFeatures and encoding

An integer that selects an entry in a vocabulary or a row in an embedding table.

Indices are addresses, not quantities. Index 42 is not 'more' than index 12, and the model never does arithmetic on them; it only uses them to fetch a vector. Some indices are reserved, such as 0 for padding and 1 for unknown.

Example In the worked example A42 → 42 and shoes → 2. Index 2 in the category table and index 2 in the device table refer to unrelated rows.

See also: Vocabulary, Embedding table, Reserved index, Label encoding

IntegerMath and notation

A whole number with no fractional part, such as 0, 7, or 42.

Vocabulary indices, counts, and lengths are integers. Index tensors are typically stored as 32- or 64-bit integer types; using a float type for indices is a common bug that frameworks reject.

Example history_item_ids = [[12, 18, 33, 0, 0]] is an integer tensor; dense = [[0.80, 0.391]] is a float tensor.

See also: Index, Floating-point number, Tensor

InteractionBasics

Any logged action by a user on an item, such as a view, click, add-to-cart, purchase, or rating.

Interactions are the raw material of recommendations: past interactions become history features, and future interactions become labels. Each interaction type has its own meaning and strength of signal.

Example U7 viewing A12 at 09:40 is an interaction; so is U7 clicking A42 at 10:00:05.

See also: History, Implicit feedback, Click, Label

Invalid clickAds and business

A click that is filtered out and not billed or used as a positive label, for example from a bot, fraud, or an accidental double tap.

Ads platforms filter invalid clicks so advertisers are not charged for them. Training labels should use the same filtering, so the model predicts valid, billable clicks. Filtering may happen with a delay, which is another reason labels need time to become final.

Example Two clicks on imp_101 arrive 50 ms apart from the same device. The second is treated as an accidental duplicate and ignored.

See also: Click, Deduplication, CPC, Label finalization

Inverse-probability weightingLabels and sampling

Giving each kept example a weight of 1/q, where q was its probability of being kept, so the sample represents the original population.

If only 1 in 99 negatives is kept, each kept negative stands in for 99. Weighting it by 99 restores the original balance in the loss and in metrics. The weights are correct only if q is the true sampling probability recorded at sampling time.

Example Keep all 1,000 clicks (q = 1, weight 1) and 1,000 of 99,000 non-clicks (q = 1/99, weight 99). Weighted negatives total 1,000 × 99 = 99,000, the original count.

See also: Sample probability, Sample weight, Downsampling, Calibration

ISO 8601Data formats

The international standard format for writing dates and times, such as 2026-11-01T10:00:05Z.

The format goes from the largest unit to the smallest: year-month-day, a T, then hours:minutes:seconds, then a time zone. A trailing Z means UTC; otherwise an offset such as +08:00 is given. Because it sorts correctly as text and is unambiguous, it is widely used in logs.

Example 2026-11-01T09:59:58Z means November 1, 2026, at 9:59:58 in UTC.

See also: Timestamp, UTC

ItemBasics

The thing being recommended: an ad, product, video, article, song, or anything else the system can show.

Each item has an identity (item ID) and descriptive attributes (category, price, text, images). Items are candidates while being considered, and become impressions when shown.

Example A42 is a running-shoe ad; A81 is a camera ad; A33 is a book.

See also: Candidate, Impression, Content feature

JoinLogs and joins

Combining rows from two or more tables by matching a shared key, such as impression_id or item_id.

Training rows are assembled by joining impressions with clicks, request context, item attributes, and user history. The join key and matching rule decide which information ends up together, so a sloppy join can attach the wrong click or the wrong version of an item.

Example Join Impressions to Clicks on impression_id: imp_101 matches the click at 10:00:05; imp_102 matches nothing, so after finalization its label is 0.

Watch out Joining clicks on (user_id, item_id) instead of impression_id can attach one click to every showing of that ad to that user.

See also: Point-in-time join, Identifier, Attribution, Deduplication

Joint probabilityMath and notation

The probability that two events both happen, written P(A and B).

A joint probability can be built from a chain of conditional probabilities: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A). In ads, P(click and conversion) = P(click) × P(conversion | click), which is how pCTR and post-click pCVR combine into pCTCVR.

Example pCTR = 0.02 and post-click pCVR = 0.10 give P(click and conversion) = 0.002, i.e., 2 click-attributed conversions per 1,000 impressions.

See also: Conditional probability, pCTCVR, pCTR, pCVR

JSONData formats

A text format for structured data using named fields, nested objects, lists, numbers, true/false, and null.

JSON is easy for people to read and naturally holds nested records, such as a list of history events inside one training example. It distinguishes numbers from strings and has an explicit null for missing values. It is bulkier and slower to scan than columnar formats like Parquet.

Example {"user_id": "U7", "candidate_price": 80.0, "recent_history": [{"item_id": "A12"}], "labels": {"clicked": 1}}

See also: CSV, Parquet, Schema, Missing value

LabelBasics

The observed outcome the model learns to predict, often written y; also called the target.

For click prediction, y = 1 means the impression received a valid attributed click within the window and y = 0 means it did not. The label comes from events after the prediction, so it exists only in training and evaluation data. At serving time it is unknown, and that is the whole point of predicting it.

Example imp_101 has clicked = 1; imp_102 has clicked = 0 once its window has closed.

Watch out The label must never leak into the features, directly or through a history or count that includes the outcome.

See also: Feature, Positive example, Negative example, Label finalization, Attribution

Label encodingFeatures and encoding

Turning each distinct category value into an integer index (0, 1, 2, …), as in scikit-learn's LabelEncoder.

Despite the name, this usually encodes features, not labels. The fitted mapping must be saved and reused unchanged. Simple label encoders often have no slot for unseen values, so new categories at serving time need an explicit rule.

Example In the Criteo demo, the first row's C1, C2, and C3 values encode to 0, 4, and 96. Those integers are just positions in sorted vocabularies, with no meaning of their own.

Watch out Refitting the encoder on new data can renumber every category, silently scrambling which embedding belongs to which value.

See also: Vocabulary, Index, Out of vocabulary, Fitting

Label finalizationLabels and sampling

The time after which a label can no longer change: the outcome window has closed and late-arriving logs have had time to land.

Finalization time = window end + an allowance for log delay. Before that moment a missing outcome is uncertain; after it, a missing outcome is a confident negative. Recording label_finalized_at on each row makes it possible to check that no immature labels were used.

Example imp_102 shown at 10:00 with a 30-minute window and a 5-minute log allowance is finalized at 10:35.

See also: Immature label, Window, Delayed feedback, Label

Label maskLabels and sampling

A 0/1 flag per label that says whether that label is valid and should count toward the loss.

In multi-task data, some targets do not apply to every row. A conversion label is meaningless for an impression whose window is still open, and a post-click target is undefined without a click. The mask zeroes out those terms so they neither help nor hurt training.

Example clicked = 1 (mask 1), converted = 0 (mask 0, because the 7-day window is still open).

See also: Mask, Multi-task model, Immature label, Missing value

Last-click attributionAds and business

A credit rule that gives 100% of a conversion to the last ad clicked before it.

Last click is simple and easy to audit, and Criteo's attribution research describes last click within 30 days as the industry standard. It ignores earlier clicks and all views, so ads that introduce a product early in a journey get no credit. Google Ads still offers last click alongside data-driven attribution.

Example U7 clicks ad A42 on November 1 and a search ad on November 4, then buys on November 5. Last click gives the search ad credit 1 and A42 credit 0.

See also: Attribution, Multi-touch attribution, Data-driven attribution, Window

LayerModels and training

One stage of computation in a neural network, usually a weighted combination of its inputs followed by a nonlinear function.

Layers are stacked so each transforms the previous one's output. Early layers in a recommender often do embedding lookups and pooling; later layers combine everything into a final score. Each layer has its own learnable weights.

Example A layer takes the 64-number concatenated input, multiplies it by a 64 × 32 weight matrix, adds a bias, and applies a nonlinear function to produce 32 numbers.

See also: Neural network, Weight (model), Nonlinear function, Parameters

Listwise rankingRecommendation tasks

Training on a whole group of candidates from one request at once, so the loss judges their order relative to each other.

Listwise data keeps every candidate from a request together with its label, so the model is rewarded for putting better items ahead of worse ones within that list. The request grouping must be preserved, and padded candidates in a fixed-size list must be masked out.

Example request_id req_10, candidates [A42, A81, A90, PAD], labels [1, 0, 0, –], valid mask [1, 1, 1, 0].

See also: Pairwise ranking, Pointwise training, Ranking, Mask, NDCG at K

Log lossEvaluation

Binary cross-entropy averaged over examples (optionally weighted); lower is better.

Log loss rewards predictions that are both well-ranked and well-calibrated, and punishes confident mistakes severely. It is the standard training loss and a key evaluation metric for click models. Raw log loss on downsampled data is not comparable to log loss on real traffic.

Example Two examples: p = 0.20 with y = 1 (loss 1.609) and p = 0.20 with y = 0 (loss 0.223). Log loss = (1.609 + 0.223) / 2 ≈ 0.916.

See also: Binary cross-entropy, Calibration, AUC, Sample weight

Log transformFeatures and encoding

Replacing a nonnegative count x with log(1 + x) so that huge values are compressed and small differences near zero remain visible.

Counts like impressions or views are heavily skewed: most are small, a few are enormous. A log transform turns multiplicative differences into additive ones, which models handle more easily. The +1 keeps a count of 0 at 0 instead of an undefined log(0).

Example Counts 0, 9, and 999 become ln(1) = 0, ln(10) ≈ 2.30, and ln(1000) ≈ 6.91.

See also: Normalization, Natural logarithm, Dense feature

LossModels and training

A single number measuring how wrong the model's predictions are on a batch; training tries to make it smaller.

The loss function compares predictions with labels and outputs a score: zero for perfect, larger for worse. Gradient descent changes parameters in the direction that reduces it. The choice of loss defines what 'good' means, for example binary cross-entropy for click probabilities.

Example A batch with per-example losses 1.609 and 0.223 and equal weights has a loss of 0.916.

See also: Binary cross-entropy, Log loss, Gradient descent, Reduction, Sample weight

MarketplaceAds and business

The system of users, advertisers, and the platform, whose interests and actions affect one another through auctions, budgets, and prices.

Changing a ranking model in an ads system can shift which advertisers win, how fast budgets drain, what prices are paid, and what users see. These effects spill across users and advertisers, so marketplace changes need careful experiments and metrics beyond CTR.

Example A new model that favors shoe ads may spend shoe advertisers' budgets by noon, leaving afternoon traffic to camera ads.

See also: Auction, Budget, A/B test, Advertiser

MaskTensors and arrays

An array of 1/0 or True/False values marking which entries in another array are real and which are padding or invalid.

Batches need fixed-size arrays, so short lists are padded with placeholder values. The mask tells the model and the loss to ignore placeholders. Without it, padding index 0 would be averaged into the history as if it were a real event.

Example history_item_ids [12, 18, 33, 0, 0] with mask [1, 1, 1, 0, 0]: only the first three positions are used.

See also: Padding, Label mask, Boolean, History

MatrixTensors and arrays

A two-dimensional grid of numbers with rows and columns.

Matrices appear everywhere in models: a batch of feature vectors is a matrix (B rows), an embedding table is a matrix (one row per index), and layer weights are matrices. A matrix is a tensor with two dimensions.

Example dense for a batch of 3 examples is a 3 × 2 matrix: [[0.80, 0.39], [3.00, 0.39], [0.80, 0.87]].

See also: Tensor, Vector, Shape, Embedding table

MeanMath and notation

The average: add up the values and divide by how many there are.

Means appear in loss reduction (the average per-example loss), in standardization (subtracting the training mean), and in mean pooling (averaging history embeddings).

Example The mean of 1.609 and 0.223 is (1.609 + 0.223) / 2 = 0.916.

See also: Standard deviation, Reduction, Pooling, Standardization

MetadataLogs and joins

Bookkeeping fields such as event IDs, timestamps, and schema versions, used for joining, auditing, and debugging rather than prediction.

Metadata lets you trace any training row back to the raw events that produced it and check that time rules were respected. Being in the dataset does not make a field a model input; most metadata should stay out of the model.

Example impression_id, request_id, prediction_time, shown_at, and label_finalized_at are metadata in the worked example.

See also: Feature, Identifier, Data dictionary, Schema

Missing valueFeatures and encoding

A value that is unknown or was not recorded, which is a different fact from a measured zero.

'Price unknown' and 'price is $0' mean different things, so replacing missing values with 0 can mislead the model. A common approach is to fill a default and add a separate indicator feature (1 = was missing). JSON writes missing as null; CSV usually leaves the cell empty.

Example In the Criteo sample row, I1 is missing. Filling it with 0 and adding I1_missing = 1 preserves the distinction.

Watch out Missing, padding, and unknown are three different situations and need three distinct representations.

See also: Dense feature, Out of vocabulary, Padding, Data dictionary

ModelBasics

A function with adjustable numbers (parameters) that takes features x and outputs a prediction, such as a click probability.

Training sets the parameters so that predictions match labels on past data; serving applies the trained function to new requests. The model is only as good as the data it learned from and the consistency between training and serving inputs.

Example model(x for imp_101) = 0.03 means the model estimates a 3% chance that U7 clicks A42 in this context.

See also: Parameters, Neural network, Training, Serving, Prediction

Multi-task modelModels and training

One model that predicts several targets at once, such as click, conversion, and watch time, usually sharing some internal layers.

Related targets help each other: lots of click data can improve representations used for rarer conversions. Each target still needs its own definition, window, and validity mask, because not every target exists for every row.

Example Output heads predict pCTR, post-click pCVR, and expected watch time from shared user and item embeddings.

See also: Label mask, pCTR, pCVR, Watch time

Multi-touch attributionAds and business

Any credit rule that splits one conversion among several ad interactions instead of giving it all to one.

Rules-based versions use fixed formulas: first click (all to the first), linear (equal shares), time decay (more to recent interactions), and position-based (more to the first and last). Google Ads no longer supports those four and moved affected conversion actions to data-driven attribution, which learns the split from data.

Example Two qualifying clicks under linear attribution each receive 0.5 of the conversion; if a qualifying view is added, each receives one third.

See also: Last-click attribution, Data-driven attribution, Shapley value, Attribution

Natural logarithmMath and notation

The logarithm with base e ≈ 2.718, written ln; ln(x) answers 'e raised to what power equals x?'.

ln(1) = 0, ln of a number between 0 and 1 is negative, and ln shrinks toward minus infinity as x approaches 0. That last property is why binary cross-entropy gives an enormous loss to a confident wrong prediction.

Example ln(0.20) ≈ −1.609, ln(0.80) ≈ −0.223, and ln(e) = 1.

See also: Binary cross-entropy, Log transform, Sigmoid

NDCG at KEvaluation

Normalized discounted cumulative gain at K: a ranking score for the top K results that rewards relevant items more when they appear higher, scaled so a perfect ordering scores 1.

DCG adds each result's relevance divided by a discount that grows with position, commonly log2(position + 1). Dividing by the DCG of the best possible ordering (IDCG) gives a value from 0 to 1. Variants differ in the gain (relevance itself or 2^relevance − 1) and the discount, so state the formula you use.

Example Top 2 results have relevance [0, 1]. DCG = 0/log2(2) + 1/log2(3) ≈ 0.631. Ideal order [1, 0] gives 1.0. NDCG@2 ≈ 0.631.

See also: Recall at K, Ranking, Listwise ranking, Evaluation

Negative exampleLabels and sampling

A training row with label 0 under a stated outcome rule; in retrieval, a sampled item used as a contrast.

In CTR data, a negative is a real impression that received no valid click within its finalized window. It means 'not clicked this time', not 'disliked'. In retrieval, negatives are usually sampled items the user did not interact with, which may include items they would actually like.

Example imp_102 (camera ad A81 shown to U7, no click by 10:35) is a CTR negative.

Watch out Items never shown, and impressions whose window is still open, are not negatives.

See also: Positive example, Label, In-batch negative, Immature label, Candidate

Neural networkModels and training

A model built from stacked layers of weighted sums and nonlinear functions, whose weights are learned from data.

Each layer multiplies its inputs by learned weights, adds them up, and applies a nonlinear function. Stacking layers lets the network represent complex relationships between features. In recommenders, a neural network usually sits on top of embedding lookups.

Example Embeddings and dense features for imp_101 → concatenated vector → two layers → sigmoid → pCTR 0.03.

See also: Layer, Parameters, Nonlinear function, Embedding, Sigmoid

Next-item predictionRecommendation tasks

A task where the model sees a user's history up to some point and predicts which item comes next.

The label is an item identifier rather than a 0/1 outcome, so the model effectively chooses among many items. Training examples are made by cutting real histories at a point and using the next event as the target.

Example History [A12, A18, A33, A42]: input [A12, A18, A33], target A42.

See also: Causal sequence training, Sequence model, Retrieval, History

Nonlinear functionModels and training

A function whose output is not just a constant times its input plus a constant; neural networks need them to learn complex patterns.

Stacking purely linear layers collapses into one linear layer, no matter how many there are. Inserting a nonlinear function between layers breaks that collapse. A common choice is ReLU, which outputs max(0, x); sigmoid is used at the output to produce probabilities.

Example ReLU(−2) = 0 and ReLU(3) = 3. No single straight line y = a·x + b reproduces both.

See also: Neural network, Layer, Sigmoid

NormalizationFeatures and encoding

Rescaling numerical features into a convenient range, such as dividing by a constant, standardizing, or taking a log.

Features with wildly different scales (a price of 300 versus a ratio of 0.02) make training harder. Normalization puts them on comparable footing. Whatever transformation and fitted statistics you choose must be identical in training and serving.

Example candidate_price / 100 turns $80 into 0.80; hour_utc / 23 turns 9 into 0.391.

See also: Standardization, Log transform, Cyclic encoding, Fitting, Training-serving skew

Numerical stabilityMath and notation

Computing a formula in a way that avoids overflow, underflow, or loss of precision with finite computer numbers.

Directly computing ln(p) when p has rounded to exactly 0 gives minus infinity and breaks training. Libraries rearrange formulas, for example computing binary cross-entropy directly from the model's pre-sigmoid output, to keep results finite and accurate.

Example If a model outputs p = 1e−50, float32 rounds it to 0 and −ln(0) is infinite. A stable implementation still returns the correct finite loss of about 115.

See also: Binary cross-entropy, Sigmoid, Floating-point number

Offline evaluationEvaluation

Measuring a model on previously logged data, without showing anything to real users.

Offline evaluation is fast, cheap, and safe, which makes it the first filter for new models. But logged data reflects what the old system chose to show, so it says little about items the old system rarely displayed. Promising offline results are confirmed with online experiments.

Example Compute AUC and log loss of a new model on the Nov 26–30 test set.

See also: Online experiment, Selection bias, Feedback loop, Test set

One-hot vectorFeatures and encoding

A vector with one slot per vocabulary entry, containing 1 at the observed value's position and 0 everywhere else.

One-hot vectors explain conceptually what a categorical input is, but they are wasteful: with a million items, each vector has 999,999 zeros. Models instead receive the integer index; looking up an embedding row by index gives the same result as multiplying the one-hot vector by the embedding table.

Example Vocabulary [PAD, UNKNOWN, shoes, books, cameras]: shoes (index 2) = [0, 0, 1, 0, 0].

See also: Sparse feature, Index, Embedding table, Vocabulary

Online experimentEvaluation

An experiment on live traffic that compares the real-world behavior and outcomes of different system versions.

Online experiments measure what offline metrics cannot: how users, advertisers, and the marketplace respond to the changed system, including effects of the new model choosing different items to show. The most common form is an A/B test.

Example Serve the new ranking model to 5% of users for a week and compare clicks, conversions, and revenue with the other 95%.

See also: A/B test, Offline evaluation, Marketplace

Out of vocabularyFeatures and encoding

A value that is not in the fitted vocabulary, often abbreviated OOV; it is typically mapped to a reserved unknown index.

New items, new users, and rare values appear all the time after training. Without a plan, an OOV value either crashes the loader or is silently mapped onto a real category. Reserving an unknown index gives the model one learned vector for 'something I have not seen'. Hashing is an alternative.

Example New item A99 is not in the item vocabulary, so it maps to UNKNOWN → 1. Its category 'shoes' is still known and maps to 2.

See also: Reserved index, Vocabulary, Cold start, Feature hashing

OverfittingModels and training

When a model learns quirks of its training data so closely that it performs worse on new data.

An overfit model has memorized rather than generalized. It shows up as training loss continuing to fall while validation loss rises. ID embeddings for rare items are especially prone to it. Held-out validation data detects it.

Example After the third epoch, training log loss keeps dropping but validation log loss climbs from 0.45 to 0.47: the model is overfitting.

See also: Validation set, Epoch, Evaluation, Hyperparameter

PaddingTensors and arrays

Filling a short list with placeholder values so every example in a batch has the same length.

Arrays in a batch must be rectangular, but users have different numbers of past events. Padding adds a reserved value, often index 0, to fill the gap, and a mask or length tells the model which positions are real. The padding value must never be used for a real category.

Example History [12, 18, 33] padded to L = 5 becomes [12, 18, 33, 0, 0] with length 3.

See also: Mask, Truncation, Reserved index, Batch

Pairwise rankingRecommendation tasks

Training on pairs of items under the same context, teaching the model to score the preferred item above the other.

Instead of asking 'how likely is a click on this item?', pairwise training asks 'which of these two is better here?'. Pairs must share the same context, usually the same request, so the comparison is fair.

Example context = req_10, preferred_item = A42 (clicked), other_item = A81 (shown, not clicked).

See also: Listwise ranking, Pointwise training, Ranking

ParametersModels and training

The numbers inside a model that training adjusts, including layer weights and embedding vectors.

Parameters are what the model 'knows'. They start random and are updated by gradient descent to reduce the loss. Large recommenders can have billions of parameters, most of them in embedding tables. Contrast hyperparameters, which people choose.

Example The embedding [0.12, −0.40, 0.08, 0.31] for 'shoes' is four parameters.

See also: Embedding, Weight (model), Hyperparameter, Gradient descent

ParquetData formats

A binary, typed, column-oriented file format for tables, supporting nested and list-valued columns.

Parquet stores each column together, which compresses well and lets readers load only the columns they need. Unlike CSV it records each column's type, so IDs stay strings and floats stay floats. List columns, such as a history of item IDs, are stored natively.

Example A Parquet file with columns impression_id (string), candidate_price (float), and recent_history (list of structs) preserves all types exactly.

See also: CSV, JSON, Schema

pCTCVRAds and business

Predicted probability that an impression leads to both a click and a click-attributed conversion.

pCTCVR = pCTR × post-click pCVR, when both are estimated for the same impression context and the conversion definition requires the click. It is the conversion probability per impression for click-attributed conversions, and so the quantity a CPA advertiser's expected value depends on. It excludes view-through conversions.

Example pCTR 0.02 × post-click pCVR 0.10 = pCTCVR 0.002.

Watch out Multiplying pCTR by an impression-level pCVR counts the click probability twice.

See also: pCTR, pCVR, Joint probability, Post-click model, CPA

pCTRBasics

Predicted click-through rate: the model's estimated probability that this impression receives a valid click under the stated label rule.

pCTR is the model's output for one specific user, item, and context. It is meant to be read as a probability, which is only valid if the model is calibrated on the population being scored. In ads, pCTR multiplied by the bid estimates expected value per impression.

Example pCTR = 0.03 for imp_101 means about 3 in 100 comparable impressions would be clicked.

See also: CTR, Calibration, Sigmoid, eCPM, Prediction

pCVRAds and business

Predicted conversion rate; you must state whether it is conditional on a click (post-click) or on an impression.

Post-click pCVR estimates P(conversion | click, x) and is trained on clicked rows. Impression-level pCVR estimates P(conversion | x) over all impressions. The two differ by a factor of pCTR and must not be mixed up.

Example Post-click pCVR = 0.10 means 10% of clicks are expected to convert. With pCTR 0.02, impression-level pCVR = 0.002.

See also: CVR, Post-click model, pCTCVR, Conditional probability

Point-in-time joinLogs and joins

A join that, for each training row, picks only the information that was valid and available at that row's prediction time.

Attributes change: prices update, categories get corrected, users accumulate history. A point-in-time join looks up the version in effect at the cutoff instead of today's value. That requires tables with validity intervals or availability timestamps.

Example A42 cost $80 until 12:00 and $65 after. For the request scored at 09:59:58, the join picks $80, because 09:59:58 falls in [valid_from, valid_to) of that version.

Watch out Joining against the current item table uses the noon price for a 10:00 impression, which is leakage.

See also: Join, Cutoff, Available time, Data leakage, Half-open interval

Pointwise trainingRecommendation tasks

Training on one candidate at a time with its own label, then ranking candidates by their individual scores.

Most CTR models are pointwise: each impression is an independent row with a 0/1 label. The model never sees a sorted list during training, yet its scores can still be sorted to produce a ranking. Calibrated pointwise probabilities are also directly usable in ads auctions.

Example Score A42 (0.03), A81 (0.01), and A90 (0.02) independently, then show them in the order A42, A90, A81.

See also: Pairwise ranking, Listwise ranking, Ranking, pCTR

PoolingModels and training

Combining several vectors into one fixed-size summary, for example by summing, averaging, or taking a weighted sum.

A history of 3 or 50 items must become one vector the next layer can accept. Pooling does that. Sum and mean pooling ignore order and treat every event equally; attention pooling uses learned weights. Masks keep padded positions out of the pool.

Example Mean pooling of embeddings [1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1] gives [(1+0+1)/3, (0+1+1)/3] = [0.67, 0.67].

See also: Weighted sum, Attention, Mask, History

PositionAds and business

The slot where an item is displayed on the page, such as first in the feed or third from the top.

Higher positions get more attention and more clicks regardless of quality. The final position is decided after ranking, so it is usually unknown when candidates are scored. Logging it is valuable for analysis and bias correction, but using it as a feature requires a plan for what value to provide at serving time.

Example imp_101 appeared in position 1 and imp_102 in position 2 of the home feed.

See also: Position bias, Surface, Data leakage

Position biasEvaluation

The tendency for items in higher, more visible positions to receive more clicks independently of how relevant they are.

Because the old system put its favorite items on top, those items collected extra clicks partly due to placement. A model trained naively learns 'the old system liked this' as much as 'users like this'. Methods such as logging position and modeling its effect separately help reduce the bias.

Example The same ad might get 3% CTR in position 1 and 1% in position 5, even though the ad itself is identical.

See also: Position, Selection bias, Feedback loop

Positive exampleLabels and sampling

A training row with label 1 under a stated outcome rule; in retrieval, an interaction treated as relevant.

In CTR data, a positive is an impression with at least one valid, attributed click within its window. In retrieval, a positive is an observed interaction, such as a view or purchase, that the model should rank above contrasts.

Example imp_101 (A42 shown to U7, clicked at 10:00:05) is a positive.

See also: Negative example, Label, Attribution, In-batch negative

Post-click modelAds and business

A model trained only on clicked impressions to predict what happens after the click, typically conversion.

It estimates P(conversion | click, x). Its training data contains only clicked rows, but at serving time it scores candidates whose click has not happened yet. That mismatch is sample selection bias, and is a known weakness of this setup.

Example Train on 20 clicked impressions (2 converted) to predict post-click CVR, then apply it to all 1,000 candidate impressions.

See also: pCVR, Selection bias, pCTCVR, Conditional probability

PostbackAds and business

A report sent to an ad network after an attributed conversion, telling it that one of its ads won credit.

In mobile app advertising, the phone's operating system can decide attribution on the device and send the ad network a postback later. Apple's AdAttributionKit sends signed postbacks at least 24 to 48 hours after the event; Apple states they contain no user- or device-specific data. One ad network receives the winning postback, and for installs up to five others can receive non-winning ones.

Example U7 taps an app-install ad and installs within 30 days. A day or two later the ad network receives a postback saying its ad won, with a conversion value set by the app, but no information about who U7 is.

Watch out Postbacks arrive late and without user identity, so they cannot be joined to individual impression rows the way a click identifier can.

See also: Attribution, Window, Delayed feedback, Click identifier

PredictionBasics

The model's output for one input, such as an estimated click probability for one impression.

Predictions are made at serving time from features alone, before the outcome is known. During training, the same predictions are compared with known labels to compute the loss.

Example For imp_101 the model outputs 0.03; later the click arrives, so the label is 1.

See also: Model, pCTR, Prediction time, Serving

Prediction timeLogs and joins

The moment the system scores a candidate; it defines the cutoff for features and can be earlier than display time.

Scoring happens before the page is rendered, so prediction time usually precedes shown_at by milliseconds to seconds. Features must be computed as of prediction time, not shown time, because that is when the real model had to decide.

Example req_10 was scored at 09:59:58 and the impressions were shown at 10:00:00. The feature cutoff is 09:59:58, and hour_utc is 9.

See also: Cutoff, Available time, Point-in-time join, Request

PreprocessingFeatures and encoding

All the transformations applied to raw data before it reaches the model: cleaning, encoding, scaling, truncation, padding.

Preprocessing definitions are effectively part of the model. Some steps are fitted (vocabularies, means), so they must be fitted on training data only and then applied identically everywhere else, including serving.

Example Map categories to indices, divide price by 100, keep the latest 5 history events, pad with 0, and build the mask.

See also: Encoding, Fitting, Normalization, Training-serving skew, Data loader

ProbabilityMath and notation

A number from 0 to 1 expressing how likely an event is; 0 means impossible and 1 means certain.

A probability of 0.03 means that, over many comparable situations, the event happens about 3% of the time. It is a statement about frequencies, not a guarantee for any single case.

Example pCTR = 0.03: across 10,000 impressions like this one, about 300 should be clicked.

See also: Conditional probability, Joint probability, Calibration, pCTR

QueryRecommendation tasks

Everything that describes what the system is being asked for; in retrieval it includes user history and context, not just typed search text.

In a search engine the query is the typed text. In a recommender's retrieval stage, the 'query' side of a two-tower model is the user and context: who they are, what they did recently, which page they are on. The model turns the query into a vector and finds items whose vectors match.

Example Query for req_10: user U7, history [A12, A18, A33], device mobile, surface home_feed.

See also: Two-tower model, Retrieval, Context, Request

Random splitEvaluation

Dividing examples into training and evaluation sets by random assignment, ignoring time.

Random splits are convenient for demos but unrealistic for recommendation: the model gets to train on events from after some evaluation events, which never happens live. Preprocessing fitted before a random split also leaks evaluation data into training.

Example The Criteo demo fits encoders on all 200 rows, then randomly assigns 80% to training and 20% to testing. That is fine for learning mechanics, not for a production evaluation.

See also: Temporal split, Data leakage, Fitting, Test set

RankingRecommendation tasks

Scoring a set of candidates and ordering them from best to worst for display.

Ranking usually follows retrieval: retrieval narrows millions of items to hundreds, then a more detailed ranking model scores each candidate with rich features such as history and context. The top-scored items are shown, sometimes after business rules or an auction.

Example Ranking scores A42 = 0.03, A90 = 0.02, A81 = 0.01, so A42 goes in the top slot.

See also: Retrieval, Pointwise training, Pairwise ranking, Listwise ranking, Candidate

Rating predictionRecommendation tasks

A task where the model predicts the numerical rating a user would give an item.

Each training row is a user, an item, and the rating they gave. The label is a number on a scale rather than 0/1, so a loss like squared error is typical. Rating data is explicit feedback.

Example Row: user = U7, item = A42, rating = 4. The model might predict 3.6 and be penalized by (4 − 3.6)² = 0.16.

See also: Explicit feedback, Label, Pointwise training

Recall at KEvaluation

Of all items defined as relevant, the fraction that appear among the first K results.

Recall@K is the main metric for retrieval, where the job is to make sure good items reach the ranking stage at all. It ignores order within the top K. K must be stated, and 'relevant' must be defined, for example items the user later clicked.

Example A user later clicked 4 items; 2 of them appear in the top 10 retrieved. Recall@10 = 2/4 = 0.5.

See also: NDCG at K, Retrieval, Evaluation

Recurrent modelModels and training

A sequence model that reads events one at a time and updates a running summary (its state) after each one.

Because it processes events in order, a recurrent model is naturally sensitive to sequence order, unlike simple pooling. The final state summarizes the whole history and can be used as the user representation.

Example Reading [A12, A18, A33] in order, the model updates its state three times; the final state reflects all three, with order preserved.

See also: Recurrent state, Sequence model, History, Pooling

Recurrent stateModels and training

The running summary vector a recurrent model carries forward and updates after each event.

At each step the new state is computed from the previous state and the current event's embedding. The state after the last event serves as a compact summary of the whole sequence.

Example state_0 = zeros; state_1 = f(state_0, A12); state_2 = f(state_1, A18); state_3 = f(state_2, A33) summarizes U7's history.

See also: Recurrent model, Sequence model, Vector

ReductionModels and training

How per-example losses are combined into one batch loss, for example a plain mean, a sum, or a weighted sum divided by total weight.

With sample weights, 'mean of weight × loss' and 'sum of weight × loss divided by sum of weights' give different numbers whenever the weights in a batch do not average to 1. This changes how much each batch influences training. Use the convention your framework and your sampling scheme expect.

Example Losses [1.0, 2.0], weights [1, 3]. Mean of weighted losses = (1 + 6)/2 = 3.5. Weighted sum / sum of weights = 7/4 = 1.75.

See also: Loss, Sample weight, Mean, Framework

RequestBasics

One occasion on which the system is asked to choose items to show, such as a page load or a feed refresh.

A request carries the context (device, surface, time) and produces a set of scored candidates, some of which become impressions. Grouping by request_id is how listwise and pairwise data keep comparable items together.

Example req_10 was scored at 09:59:58 on mobile home_feed and produced impressions imp_101 (A42) and imp_102 (A81).

See also: Impression, Context, Prediction time, Listwise ranking

Reserved indexFeatures and encoding

A vocabulary index set aside for a special meaning, such as 0 for padding or 1 for unknown, never given to a real category.

Reserving indices keeps special situations distinct from real values: padding should be ignored, unknown should get its own learned vector. Conventions vary by library and even by feature, so document them.

Example In the worked example every vocabulary uses PAD → 0 and UNKNOWN → 1; real values start at 2. In the Criteo demo no index is reserved and 0 is a real category.

See also: Padding, Out of vocabulary, Vocabulary, Index

RetrievalRecommendation tasks

The first stage of recommendation: quickly selecting a few hundred or thousand promising candidates out of a catalog of millions.

Running a detailed ranking model on every item for every request is too slow. Retrieval uses cheaper models, often two-tower models with a dot product, to shortlist candidates fast. Its training data pairs a user or query with a relevant item and contrasting items, and it is evaluated with recall at K.

Example From 10 million ads, retrieval picks 500 for U7; ranking then scores those 500 in detail.

See also: Ranking, Two-tower model, In-batch negative, Recall at K, Query

ROC curveEvaluation

Receiver operating characteristic curve: a plot of the true positive rate against the false positive rate as the decision threshold moves from high to low.

At each threshold, the true positive rate is the share of actual positives scored above it, and the false positive rate is the share of actual negatives scored above it. Sweeping the threshold traces a curve from (0, 0) to (1, 1). The area under it is AUC. The name comes from radar signal detection.

Example At threshold 0.45 with positives scored [0.9, 0.4] and negatives [0.5, 0.1]: TPR = 1/2 (only 0.9 is above), FPR = 1/2 (only 0.5 is above).

See also: AUC, Evaluation

Sample probabilityLabels and sampling

The probability q that an eligible row was kept by the sampling procedure; recorded so the sampling can be corrected later.

If sampling depends on the label or other fields, each kept row should store its q. Inverse-probability weights (1/q) and evaluation corrections depend on it. Without it, nobody can reconstruct the original population.

Example Clicks kept with q = 1; non-clicks kept with q = 1/99 ≈ 0.0101.

See also: Inverse-probability weighting, Downsampling, Sample weight

Sample weightLabels and sampling

A multiplier that sets how much one row counts in the loss or in a metric; 1.0 means ordinary.

Weights correct for sampling (1/q), emphasize important examples, or down-weight noisy ones. They change both training and evaluation, so the weighting scheme must be documented and matched to the reduction convention.

Example A kept non-click with q = 1/99 gets weight 99; imp_101 has sample_weight 1.0.

See also: Inverse-probability weighting, Sample probability, Reduction, Loss

Sampling bias correctionLabels and sampling

Adjusting a retrieval model's training for the fact that some items are picked as negatives more often than others.

With in-batch negatives, popular items appear as contrasts far more often, so the model learns to push them down too hard. A common fix subtracts the log of each item's estimated sampling probability from its score during training (often called logQ correction), so frequently sampled items are not over-penalized.

Example If item A42 appears in 1% of batches and A90 in 0.01%, A42's training score is adjusted upward relative to A90's to compensate.

See also: In-batch negative, Retrieval, Two-tower model, Sample probability

SchemaData formats

The defined structure of a record: field names, types, nesting, and meanings.

A schema makes data predictable for every producer and consumer. When it changes (a new field, a renamed column, a changed unit) the schema version should change too, so old and new data are not silently mixed.

Example Training record schema v3: metadata {impression_id: string, prediction_time: timestamp, …}, features {…}, labels {clicked: int}, sample_weight: float.

See also: Data dictionary, Metadata, Parquet, JSON

ScoreBasics

A number a model assigns to a candidate for ordering; it may or may not be a calibrated probability.

Ranking needs only that better candidates get higher scores. Some scores, such as a calibrated pCTR, can also be read as probabilities; others, such as a dot product from a retrieval model, cannot. Do not multiply a non-probability score by a bid.

Example A two-tower dot product of 4.2 for (U7, A42) means A42 is a closer match than an item with 1.3. It does not mean a 420% click chance.

See also: pCTR, Dot product, Calibration, Ranking

Selection biasEvaluation

When the examples you observe differ systematically from the population you care about, because of how they were selected.

Recommendation logs only contain outcomes for items the old system chose to show, and post-click data only contains users who clicked. A model trained on such data can be wrong on the population it is actually applied to.

Example A post-click CVR model is trained on the 2% of impressions that were clicked, then applied to all candidates. Those who click may convert at very different rates from everyone else.

See also: Post-click model, Feedback loop, Position bias, Offline evaluation

Sequence modelModels and training

A model designed to use the order of events in a history, for example through positions, timestamps, or step-by-step processing.

Pooling throws order away; sequence models keep it. Recurrent models process events one by one; other designs add position or time information to each event's embedding and let the model relate events to each other. Order matters when recent behavior or transitions such as 'viewed, then bought' carry signal.

Example A sequence model can tell [shoes, shoes, books] from [books, shoes, shoes]; a mean pool cannot.

See also: Recurrent model, Attention, Pooling, Causal sequence training, History

Server-side conversion eventAds and business

A conversion sent from the advertiser's own server to the ad platform, rather than reported by a script running in the user's browser.

Server events can include information the browser does not have, such as offline sales, and survive browser restrictions. To identify the person, they carry hashed customer details (for example SHA-256 hashed email or phone) and any stored click identifier. When the same purchase is also reported by a browser pixel, the two reports must be deduplicated.

Example Meta's Conversions API deduplicates a pixel event and a server event for the same purchase when both carry the same event_id and event name and arrive within 48 hours of the first.

See also: Click identifier, Deduplication, Attribution, Conversion

ServingBasics

Running a trained model on live requests to produce predictions; also called inference.

At serving time the system has features but not labels, and it must respond quickly, often within milliseconds. Every feature and preprocessing step used in training must be reproducible here with the same definitions.

Example When U7 opens the home feed, the serving system builds x for each candidate, runs the model, and ranks by pCTR.

See also: Prediction, Training-serving skew, Prediction time, Model

ShapeTensors and arrays

The size of an array along each of its dimensions, written like B × 5.

Shapes must match what the model expects; mismatches are among the most common errors. Writing shapes down for every input is the quickest way to check a data pipeline.

Example history_item_ids has shape B × 5; with B = 32 that is 32 rows of 5 indices. A click label of shape B × 1 has 32 rows of one value each.

See also: Tensor, Dimension, Batch

Shapley valueMath and notation

A method from cooperative game theory for dividing a shared result fairly among participants, by averaging each one's added contribution over every order in which participants could join.

In attribution, the 'participants' are ad channels or touchpoints and the 'result' is the conversion probability. A channel's Shapley value is its average increase in conversion probability when added to every possible subset of the other channels. Dalessandro and colleagues (2012) applied it to advertising attribution.

Example If no ads give a 0% conversion rate, search alone gives 2%, display alone 1%, and both together 4%, search's Shapley share is the average of 2% (added first) and 4% − 1% = 3% (added second), which is 2.5 points. Display gets 1.5 points; the shares sum to the 4% total.

See also: Data-driven attribution, Multi-touch attribution

SigmoidModels and training

The function σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)), which squashes any real number into a value between 0 and 1.

Click models usually end with a raw number z (any value from very negative to very positive) and pass it through a sigmoid to get a probability. z = 0 gives 0.5, large positive z approaches 1, and large negative z approaches 0.

Example σ(0) = 0.5; σ(−3.48) ≈ 0.03; σ(3) ≈ 0.95.

See also: pCTR, Binary cross-entropy, Nonlinear function, Numerical stability

Sparse featureFeatures and encoding

A categorical feature whose conceptual one-hot vector is almost all zeros; the model receives its compact integer index instead.

'Sparse' describes the one-hot representation: with a million possible items, only one slot is 1. Systems never build that vector; they pass the index and look up an embedding. In ads systems, 'sparse features' and 'categorical ID features' usually mean the same thing.

Example candidate_item_id A42 is sparse: conceptually a million-length vector with a single 1, in practice the index 42.

See also: Dense feature, One-hot vector, Categorical feature, Embedding table

Standard deviationMath and notation

A measure of how spread out values are around their mean, in the same units as the values.

Compute the average squared distance from the mean, then take the square root. In standardization, dividing by the standard deviation puts features with different units on a similar scale.

Example Prices $50, $100, $150 have mean $100 and (population) standard deviation ≈ $40.8.

See also: Mean, Standardization, Normalization

StandardizationFeatures and encoding

Rescaling a numerical feature as (x − mean) / standard deviation, using statistics fitted on training data.

After standardization a feature has mean 0 and standard deviation 1 on the training set, so features in very different units become comparable. The mean and standard deviation must come from training data only and be reused at serving.

Example Training prices have mean $100 and standard deviation $50. A42's $80 becomes (80 − 100)/50 = −0.4.

See also: Normalization, Mean, Standard deviation, Fitting

SurfaceBasics

The product location where items appear, such as the home feed, search results page, or a sidebar placement.

Users behave very differently on different surfaces, so surface is usually an important context feature. It also determines the layout, how many slots there are, and what counts as an impression.

Example req_10 came from surface = home_feed, which maps to index 2.

See also: Context, Position, Request

TargetingAds and business

Rules set by an advertiser that limit which users or contexts their ads may be shown to.

Targeting decides eligibility before scoring: an ad targeted to mobile users is never a candidate on desktop. This shapes the training data, because each ad's impressions come only from its targeted audience.

Example Ad A42 targets mobile users in a set of countries, so U9 on desktop never sees it as a candidate.

See also: Advertiser, Candidate, Selection bias

Temporal splitEvaluation

Dividing data by time: train on older events, validate on a later period, and test on a still later one.

A temporal split mimics real deployment, where a model trained on the past predicts the future. It catches problems a random split hides, such as new items and changing behavior. It does not by itself prevent leakage from immature labels, which must be checked separately.

Example Train: Nov 1–20. Validation: Nov 21–25. Test: Nov 26–30.

See also: Random split, Validation set, Test set, Immature label

TensorTensors and arrays

A numerical array with a shape and a data type; the form in which models receive data.

A single number is a 0-dimensional tensor, a vector is 1-dimensional, a matrix is 2-dimensional, and so on. Every model input, such as IDs, dense features, histories, masks, and labels, becomes a tensor with an agreed shape and type.

Example history_mask = [[True, True, True, False, False]] is a boolean tensor of shape 1 × 5.

See also: Shape, Dimension, Vector, Matrix, Float32, Batch

Test setEvaluation

Held-out examples used once, at the end, to report how well the final chosen model performs.

The test set is used for neither training nor choosing settings, so its result is an honest estimate. Repeatedly checking the test set while tuning turns it into a second validation set and makes the reported number optimistic. For probability metrics it should reflect real traffic, not be downsampled.

Example After choosing the best model on Nov 21–25 validation data, report its AUC and log loss once on Nov 26–30.

See also: Validation set, Temporal split, Evaluation, Overfitting

TimestampLogs and joins

A recorded date and time attached to an event, such as when it occurred or when it became available.

Timestamps are what make point-in-time correctness possible. Training rows typically carry several: prediction_time, shown_at, clicked_at, available_at, label_finalized_at. Keep them in one time zone, usually UTC, to avoid off-by-hours bugs.

Example shown_at = 2026-11-01T10:00:00Z for imp_101.

See also: UTC, ISO 8601, Available time, Prediction time

TokenFeatures and encoding

A small unit of text, such as a word or piece of a word, that a text model processes.

Text models first split a string into tokens, map each to an index in a token vocabulary, and look up embeddings, the same pattern as categorical features. An item title can be fed to the recommender as tokens or as a single vector from a text encoder.

Example 'Lightweight running shoe' might become tokens ['Light', 'weight', 'running', 'shoe'].

See also: Encoder, Vocabulary, Content feature

TrainingModels and training

The process of adjusting a model's parameters so its predictions match labels in historical data.

Training repeatedly takes a batch, computes predictions, measures the loss against the labels, and updates parameters by gradient descent. It uses the training split only; the validation and test splits are kept aside to check the result.

Example Each step: prediction = model(x); loss = mean(weight × BCE(prediction, y)); update parameters to reduce loss.

See also: Gradient descent, Loss, Batch, Epoch, Parameters

Training-serving skewFeatures and encoding

Any difference between how inputs are produced for training and how they are produced live, which makes the live model see unfamiliar data.

Skew arises when training and serving use different code, different vocabularies, different scaling statistics, different history rules, or different data sources. The model then receives inputs at serving time that mean something different from what it learned on. Sharing preprocessing code and logging serving features both help.

Example Training divides price by 100, but the serving code passes raw dollars. The model sees 80.0 instead of 0.80 and its predictions become nonsense.

See also: Preprocessing, Encoding, Serving, Data loader, Normalization

TruncationTensors and arrays

Keeping only part of a list, such as the most recent L events, to bound its length.

Histories can be thousands of events long, but models need a fixed maximum. Truncation decides which events survive, usually the most recent. The rule and L must be documented and identical in training and serving.

Example With L = 5 and a history of 8 events, keep the 5 most recent and drop the 3 oldest.

See also: Padding, History, Mask

Two-tower modelModels and training

A retrieval model with two separate networks: one turns the user and context into a vector, the other turns an item into a vector; their dot product is the match score.

Because the towers are separate, item vectors can be computed in advance for the whole catalog and searched quickly with a nearest-neighbor index. The cost is that the user and item never interact inside the model, so two-tower models are less precise than full ranking models.

Example User tower(U7, history, mobile) → [0.5, 1.0]; item tower(A42) → [0.2, 0.4]; score = 0.5×0.2 + 1.0×0.4 = 0.5.

See also: Retrieval, Dot product, Query, In-batch negative, Score

UTCData formats

Coordinated Universal Time, the worldwide reference time with no daylight saving; a trailing Z on a timestamp means UTC.

Storing all log times in UTC avoids confusion across time zones and daylight-saving changes. Local time can still be derived as a feature when daily patterns matter.

Example 2026-11-01T10:00:00Z is 10:00 UTC, which is 18:00 in Singapore (UTC+8).

See also: Timestamp, ISO 8601, Cyclic encoding

Validation setEvaluation

Held-out examples used to compare models and choose settings before the final test.

Training data shows how well the model memorized; validation data shows how well it generalizes. You use it to pick hyperparameters, decide when to stop training, and choose between model versions. Because you make decisions with it, a separate test set is needed for an unbiased final number.

Example Try embedding sizes 16, 32, and 64; pick 32 because it gives the lowest log loss on Nov 21–25 validation data.

See also: Test set, Hyperparameter, Overfitting, Temporal split

VectorMath and notation

An ordered list of numbers, such as an embedding or a row of dense features.

The position of each number matters: the second entry always means the same thing across vectors of the same kind. Vectors are combined by concatenation, weighted sums, and dot products.

Example [0.12, −0.40, 0.08, 0.31] is a 4-dimensional vector.

See also: Embedding, Dot product, Concatenate, Tensor

View-through conversionAds and business

A conversion credited to an impression even though the user never clicked it.

Someone may see an ad, not click, and buy later. Some attribution rules credit that impression. Such conversions are not covered by pCTR × post-click pCVR, which only counts click-attributed conversions. Platforms keep view-through windows short: Google Ads defaults to 1 day, Meta offers 1 day, and Apple's AdAttributionKit gives 24 hours from an ad view to an install.

Example U9 sees ad A42 at 20:00 without clicking and buys the shoes the next morning. Under a 1-day view-through rule, that impression gets conversion credit.

See also: Conversion, Attribution, Engaged-view conversion, pCTCVR

VocabularyFeatures and encoding

The set of known values for a categorical feature together with the mapping from each value to an integer index.

A vocabulary is fitted on training data, saved with the model, and reused unchanged at serving. It should include reserved entries for padding and unknown values. Each feature normally has its own vocabulary, though candidate and history item IDs often share one.

Example Category vocabulary: PAD → 0, UNKNOWN → 1, shoes → 2, books → 3, cameras → 4.

See also: Index, Label encoding, Out of vocabulary, Reserved index, Embedding table

Watch timeRecommendation tasks

How long a user spends viewing an item such as a video; often used as a numerical training target.

Clicks can be misleading for video: a clickbait thumbnail gets clicks but short views. Watch time captures engagement after the click. It is a numerical target, often only defined for clicked or started items, so it needs its own validity mask in a multi-task record.

Example U7 opens a video and watches 95 seconds: watch_time = 95, mask = 1. An unclicked impression has mask = 0 for watch time.

See also: Multi-task model, Label mask, Implicit feedback

Weight (model)Models and training

A learned number inside a neural network layer that multiplies an input; not the same thing as a sample weight.

Layer weights and embeddings are the model's parameters. A sample weight, by contrast, is a per-row number in the data that scales that row's loss. The two share a word but have nothing else in common.

Example A layer computes 0.4 × price_feature + (−1.2) × hour_feature + …; 0.4 and −1.2 are model weights.

See also: Parameters, Layer, Sample weight

Weighted sumMath and notation

Multiply each value (or vector) by its weight and add up the results.

Weighted sums appear in layer computations, in attention pooling over histories, and in weighted losses. A plain average is a weighted sum where every weight is 1/n.

Example Vectors [1, 0] and [0, 1] with weights 0.8 and 0.2 give 0.8×[1, 0] + 0.2×[0, 1] = [0.8, 0.2].

See also: Pooling, Attention, Mean, DIN

WindowLabels and sampling

A defined time interval, anchored to a specific event, during which an outcome counts toward a label.

A window needs four things: the anchor event (impression shown, click time), the length, whether each endpoint is included, and the allowance for late logs before the label is final. Different targets usually have different windows. In ads reporting, the window after an ad interaction is also called a lookback or conversion window. Platforms set defaults: Google Ads uses 30 days for clicks and 1 day for views unless changed.

Example Click window: starts at shown_at (10:00:00, included), lasts 30 minutes (10:30:00 excluded), plus a 5-minute log allowance, so the label is final at 10:35.

See also: Half-open interval, Attribution, Label finalization, Immature label, Engaged-view conversion

Check your understanding

Is an item that was never shown a negative CTR example?

No. There is no observed response to that showing. Retrieval may use sampled unobserved items as contrasts, which is a different objective.

Does item ID 100 have twice the meaning of item ID 50?

No. IDs identify categories. They are embedding indices, not measurements.

Can the current click appear in the history used to predict it?

No. That puts the answer into the features and leaks future information.

Is the label passed to the model at serving time?

No. The model receives features. The outcome is not yet known.

Can a one-hour-old impression be a final negative for a seven-day conversion target?

No. Its conversion window is still open. Wait, mask it, or use a method that handles delayed outcomes.

Examples are synthetic unless explicitly attributed. Real samples link to their original files.
